Specifically, we demonstrate that by using $Y_1$-measurement, one can achieve $I$-fidelity that matches the fidelity of the $G$ matrix, making it an effective tool for detecting entanglement. Furthermore, we show through both theoretical and experimental means (with a simple two-qubit optical setup) that our method can precisely measure entanglement even at low photon numbers and reliably distinguish $Y_1$- and $Y_2$-measurements.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTMs) observed on the JET tokamak have been difficult to pinpoint in terms of mode structure, but recent studies using jet-referenced ECE data have provided clearer evidence. The team combining TJEX and JET ECE data has now separately measured PTMs with jet-referenced approaches, allowing them to confirm the unique properties of these modes compared to standard neutron imaging data. They found that PTMs exhibit a toroidal structure, and comparison with linear gyrokinetic analysis suggests that PTMs can be classified as a type of localized symmetric mode (LM). Furthermore, it's hypothesized that a change in the direction of the magnetic field at a low density point may be responsible for the emergence of PTMs when this low density point is crossed during a discharge.

A basic approach that questions the use of pre-trained models in continual learning by using a data augmentation technique called Mixup has been developed. This method, known as the Mixup Baseline, does not rely on any additional modules, hyperparameters, or the use of extra data. The baseline's performance was compared across various benchmarks, bear-ing in mind the constraints of using akin models on continuous learning datasets. The results demonstrated that the Mixup baseline's performance surpassed the random baseline, and in many cases, outperformed the established Continual Learning architectures. This discovery implies that the success of pre-trained models may not be as significant as previously thought, and the Mixup baseline serves as a simple and efficient solution for many problems, including the use of a single model for multiple domains.

Our proposed approach integrates multimodal interpretations across恨 speech detection tasks, enabling the analysis of hate speech from multiple understanding perspectives (i.e., multimodal). This integration uncovers the limitations of hate speech detection models and highlights the significance of modality-specific and cross-modality interactions (i.e., text-image, text-video). Building on these insights, we introduce a novel multimodal-guided interpretable hate speech detection framework (MMG-ISH), which leverages the combination of text-image and text-video understanding tasks to enhance the effectiveness of hate speech detection. Additionally, a public dataset (DigiSpeak-20) is made available for hate speech detection research and evaluation, which consists of 50k user-generated comments (i.e., 25k hate speech and 25k non-hate speech) paired with multimedia (i.e., 25k image and 25k video) from the DigiSpeak corpus (i.e., a keyword-based hate speech detection benchmark for social media data). Our experimental results indicate the efficacy of the MMG-ISH framework, which correctly identifies hate speech with 72.11% accuracy and 74.1% precision on DigiSpeak-20. The dataset and code are accessible at https://github.com/iamkaran/Interpretable-Multimodal-Hate-Speech-Detection.

We investigate how network structure influences the behavior of a complex network of neurons using an analytical approach. By employing mean-field theory, we examine the behavior of a network where the number of synapses between neurons follows a statistical distribution, and the number of synapses per neuron also follows a probability distribution. We derive equations to describe the network's dynamics and analyze its behavior in terms of oscillation patterns and stable states. Notably, our study reveals that network topology has a significant effect on the network's behavior, particularly when the network's average connection per neuron is above a certain threshold. However, mean-field theory's accuracy is contingent upon the distribution of numbers of synapses per neuron having a specific characteristic width.

Recent years have seen the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) 
in generating high-quality data across multiple domains. Our study focuses on 
extending the effectiveness of GANs to automatic program repair, where we define 
a novel evaluation framework to compare different approaches. We develop a 
Generative Adversarial Patch Generation (GAPG) method utilizing GANs to create 
program patches that improve the accuracy of repair tools. Experimental results 
reveal that integrating program patches generated by GAPG with repair tools 
outperforms their unmodified counterparts by up to 18% in multiple evaluation 
metrics.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of the vector Gaussian vector function channel (GIFC) using a single-input, multiple-output structure. By employing an information spectrum approach, it establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the reliability of information transmission through GIFCs. The approach considers vector functions with potentially different output dimensions, linked by memoryless constraints. A specific GIFC model is developed, revealing that GIFC capacity is equivalent to the mutual information between the channel input and output variables. The results are applicable to various channels, including erasure and degradation channels, with the framework also allowing for the derivation of the capacity region of the compound GIFC.

We aim to introduce a new method called event-stamped flow analysis for studying 3-dimensional flow patterns in heavy-ion collisions. The concept of flow analysis, widely used in interpreting collision outcomes, is based on the theoretical flow equations that describe how particles in the collision behave. By examining experimentally obtained flow patterns and comparing them with theoretical predictions derived from simulation models, we can gain insights into the characteristics of the colliding systems. The novel technique, called event-stamped analysis, allows for a detailed understanding of 3D flow patterns, providing more constraints on the Equation-of-State. The event-stamped analysis method involves breaking down the 3D spatial coordinates into one-dimensional projections and analyzing these patterns as a function of the polar angle. The technique has been tested using simulated data and the results indicate that both 1-dimensional and multi-dimensional (up to N-dimensional) patterns can be used to determine the Equation-of-State. The accuracy of this simulation has been evaluated by comparing it with theoretical models and the simulated results reveal that even utilizing single-projection data can yield comparable constraints on the Equation-of-State as real-world data.

The rapid spread of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused a global pandemic, making the rapid detection of COVID-19 and monitoring its progression highly dependent on medical imaging and analysis. However, previous research involving imaging data has neglected addressing data privacy issues. Adversarial attacks and adversarial training have been proposed as a solution to protect against leaks of sensitive information, and we apply these techniques to a deep neural network for analyzing chest X-ray images. The network's ability to resist adversarial attacks increases by 10 times after implementing adversarial training compared to standard training methods, and we demonstrate that it can also be used to detect and prevent attacks.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) based machine learning model is an ideal fit for handling wireless communication systems, especially when dealing with large graphs like those representing wireless networks. However, a major challenge with GNNs is their lack of adaptability to changes in these networks over time. To overcome this limitation, a new decentralized learning approach is developed to train and adapt gNNs in response to changing graphs within wireless communication systems. Unlike traditional GNN training methods that are centralized and rely on centralized data, this new approach is decentralized, which means it can utilize the local measurements of each node. As a result, it's able to train gNNs locally using the same optimization methods as the centralized approach. To further speed up this process and reduce computation, the proposed method incorporates computation caching to leverage recurring calculations. A numerical case study is presented to compare the efficacy of both the proposed decentralized approach and the traditional centralized method, which reveals that the proposed method is faster and more efficient, especially when dealing with large and complex graphs.

The high prevalence of violent crime, particularly homicide, in the Brazilian state of Goias has prompted our comprehensive data analysis. Using comprehensive homicide rate statistics, we investigated the spatial distribution of crimes across 139 municipal regions over an 11-year span. Our methodology combined spatial autocorrelation analysis with cluster detection to reveal patterns in crime distribution. The findings suggest a notable rise in criminal activity over the studied time period, with significant spatial concentration evident. Notably, high-risk zones persisted throughout, while medium-risk areas became more prominent. The research highlights the critical need for further investigation into underlying causes of violence and its potential policy implications, aiming to inform more effective crime prevention strategies in Goias.

Our goal is to create fast and both problem-driven and error-driven variations of stochastic gradient descent. In areas such as robotics, engineering, and statistics, noise often arises due to sensor inaccuracies, measurement errors, or environmental unpredictability, which standard gradient descent methods cannot effectively handle. In contrast, robust gradient descent techniques can mitigate noise influence but typically converge slowly, losing out on the speed advantages of traditional methods in homogeneous noise environments. To tackle this issue, we developed a new algorithm, nAd SGD, that dynamically adjusts to both the type of noise and problem characteristics to accelerate convergence when noise is consistent and address noisy conditions more effectively than existing methods. Furthermore, we created an expanded version of nAd SGD, called nAd SGD+, which provides theoretical assurance of convergence even with limited sample sizes, and statistically identifies noise-present regions, ultimately achieving a balance between speed and accuracy.

Axion-like particles have emerged as the leading hypothesis explaining the axion's role in solving the strong CP problem. Although not strictly necessary, their potential existence extends beyond that of the axion. An opportunity arises to investigate axion-like particles within the Sun's core through the directionally-sensitive Axion Frame with an X-ray scanner and Oscillating magnet (WAXO) and specifically, through its development stage BabyIAXO. The prediction for their detection in the energy range of 6-15 keV, assuming a flux of $10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ and oscillation length of 1 cm, yields a sensitivity to the mixing angle of $\sim^{6\times10^{-11}}_{-\,-5\times10^{-12}}^{+8\times10^{-12}}$. This detection sensitivity significantly surpasses that of previous searches for solar axion-like particles.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two degrees of freedom, lacks equilibrium. Such a system serves as a means to establish dynamic memory, establishing it as an alternative to oscillators disconnected from a heat bath. This research establishes a connection between two studies on self-oscillating oscillators: classical mechanical oscillators and quantum oscillators with one or two degrees of freedom. These systems serve as examples of non-equilibrium dynamic memory devices.

Developing a universal grasping approach for objects is a critical challenge in both human and robotic vision due to the vast diversity of objects and the need to generalize across different types. Despite numerous datasets that facilitate learning grasping strategies, simulating dexterous manipulation becomes increasingly complex. To address this issue, this study presents an innovative dataset simulation approach utilizing the PyBullet physics engine and introduces the DexGraspNet dataset. Notably, our proposed dataset, consisting of over 150,000 simulations and 80,000 images, surpasses existing datasets in terms of diversity and covers a wide range of objects. To facilitate grasping manipulation, our approach allows for modeling flexible fingers and joint actuation rather than fixed finger poses. Furthermore, the dataset simulates realistic sensor inputs to train and test grasping algorithms, including state-of-the-art methods like single-layer and stacked multi-layered convolutional neural networks, resulting in impressive results with a 9.6% increase in success rate and a 35.4% reduction in collision rate compared to previous datasets.

A novel method utilizing free-breathing navigation in 4D MRI, which employs turbo spin-echo sequences, is introduced. The respiration signal in this sequence is projected onto its long echo-train to minimize sensitivity fluctuations. A self-corrective navigation approach is incorporated to mitigate navigation signal degradation, enabling the acquisition of high-resolution dynamic images and radial in-plane k-space sampling to enhance motion-prone abdominal imaging. The technique is showcased in its 3D format with an echo-train length of 440, achieving a spatial resolution of 1.5 mm and a 100 Hz respiration gating. The resulting in-phase and quadrature-phase (QP) images demonstrate superior structural clarity over non-structured imaging methods. The technique's advantages include the absence of ECG and respiration triggers, the ability to capture in-plane motion, and the capability to capture arterial structures, making it particularly suitable for body imaging in inhomogeneous abdominal regions.

We introduce InDistill, a novel model compression method based on knowledge distillation, aiming to preserve information flow from the teacher model to the distilled model. Traditional knowledge distillation aggregates information across channels, whereas InDistill does so spatially, maintaining critical relationships between channels. As a result, InDistill enhances the performance of downstream tasks compared to existing approaches. We demonstrate this by showing that InDistill achieves superior image classification accuracy, faster inference, and reduced model size, outperforming current state-of-the-art distillation methods using the VGG16 model, which we train using PyTorch on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-2012 datasets.

Two submersion functions defined on the two-dimensional real number space are considered; it's demonstrated that the topological equivalence of these functions is equivalent to the topological conjugacy of their respective horizontal foliations, except possibly for orbits located at infinity.

Ecosystems' biomass dynamics influenced by herbivory have been extensively studied using various models, with a primary emphasis on models incorporating localized grazing. Notwithstanding, a significant aspect of model development often goes overlooked, which involves establishing whether and to what extent model outcomes are sensitive to specific functional choices regarding mortality rates and resource renewal rates. In this context, we employ a well-established model that integrates non-local grazing and explore its mathematical characteristics, examining how biomass equilibrium and system stability are affected by various parameters, including predator mortality, which may vary within a certain threshold to ensure ecosystem survival. Furthermore, we examine the system's bifurcation behavior as we adjust the parameters and uncover notable phenomena, such as a secondary Hopf bifurcation, which is absent in models restricted to local grazing alone. Our work aims to provide a foundation for a deeper understanding of open ecosystems' dynamics governed by herbivory and to stimulate future research into these complex systems.

A novel count sketch variant is introduced that is resilient to manipulations by an adversarial input source, sacrificing a factor of $O(\log n)$ for accuracy in doing so. In contrast, standard count sketch data structures are vulnerable to specific bad choices, resulting in substantial errors, as demonstrated by a lower bound of $O(1)$.

A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its implementation on central and graphical processing units and interfacing with PySCF. When running on single-threaded sequential and accelerated parallel GPUs, it has achieved performance comparable to leading C-based codes and partial mesh AFQMC, respectively.

High-frequency trading could benefit from quantum strategies in the game theory concept known as the Prisoner's Dilemma. By implementing quantum movements that combine multiple states, we can achieve a superior outcome over traditional strategies in a short time frame. A study using IBM's quantum computer showed that a specific sequence of frequencies of quantum movements outperforms established strategies in most instances. Moreover, we discovered that market behavior, specifically earnings per share in public corporations, correlates closely with the probability of choosing a non-cooperative outcome in this game.

We investigate a two-stage mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations. In the initial stage, the seller, who lacks knowledge of buyers' valuations, must invite intermediaries to attend a auction where they can acquire an item of choice for a buyer they personally know, paying a fixed commission for each participation. Only those intermediaries who agree to pay a fixed commission will reveal their valuation for that item to the seller. In our proposed mechanism, we demonstrate that the seller can achieve a certain expected revenue, denoted as $\alpha$, when selling a single item of value $v$, in the presence of $m$ intermediaries and $f$ fixed costs, and that this result can be attained within a polynomial time frame, while showing that this result cannot be exceeded to any degree of precision, given a polynomial number of intermediaries and $f$. Furthermore, when selling $k$ items, we reveal that the seller can reach an expected $\alpha$-approximation of the optimal revenue in a polynomial time frame, but also that no better than a constant factor of $\alpha$ can be guaranteed across all scenarios involving numerous intermediaries and $f$.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've developed an automated planning system based on prompt engineering, which utilizes a pre-trained transformer model, specifically BART, fine-tuned on the PubMed dataset. We've adapted existing visual perception prompt designs for natural language processing and integrated them with BART, which had been heavily modified for summarization purposes. Initially, BART lacked the capability to generate fluent summaries and was even unable to reproduce existing text. In contrast, the novel entity-based planning approach has yielded substantial enhancements, resulting in significant gains in summarization quality as measured by ROUGE scores, while also enabling BART to produce human-like rephraseings and maintain logical coherence. Our experimental outcomes reveal that this straightforward planning strategy is highly effective, outperforming previous approaches in terms of simplicity and performance gains.

This research establishes a novel theorem of differentiation, which draws inspiration from Leibniz's introduction of induction. The theorem's contents are now being used as supplementary material in higher mathematics education. Based on this innovation, we have developed new approaches to characterize the differentiability of a function, which in turn provide simpler methods for determining the differentiability of a multivariate function. Additionally, this innovation has facilitated the reproof of a well-known theorem in higher mathematics, namely Schwarz's Theorem.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions is a crucial aspect of emotional and cognitive connection, often subtly signaling cognitive alignment and emotional bonding. By analyzing conversation patterns, researchers have established connections between synchronization and established cognitive connections, such as attention and memory. Existing models of synchronization have primarily focused on linear patterns, ignoring the dynamic nature of human interactions. In contrast, this research explores the utility of dynamic neural network models in capturing the context-dependent nature of human conversation, using audio recordings of dyadic interactions as data. By evaluating different dynamic neural network configurations, such as recurrent, Elman, WTN, and Convolutional networks, against a more traditional linear regression model, researchers discovered the advantage of context-awareness, such as the improved performance of the MCTC architecture. Furthermore, researchers found that the MCTC model exhibited robust generalizability across various conversation contexts, outperforming a linear baseline and lineary embedded GRU networks, providing new insights into the study of human communication through the use of machine learning techniques.

A recent study applied a higher-ordered multilinear model of the lambda calculus to establish a fundamental principle in quantum computing, specifically that any quantum logic gate can be constructed using a combination of the Hadamard, the T gate, and the CNOT gate. Building upon this, we demonstrate a similar result in the context of multi-qubit gates by combining the Lambda model with Stochastic mechanics, which yields a theory that uses the Lambda-S1 model. A key assumption in this process is the inclusion of the S, H, and CNOT gates. Furthermore, the model reveals a fundamental principle in both quantum computing and process algebra: the equivalence of communicating systems. We utilized this insight to redefine the CNOT gate in terms of the other quantum gates by expressing its behavior as a communication between the control and target states. A key aspect of the model involves the development of a communication operator, which allows us to express the CNOT gate using the other quantum gates. A crucial aspect of the model is the communication operator, which allows us to express the CNOT gate using the other quantum gates. A crucial aspect of the model is the communication operator, which allows us to express the CNOT gate using the other quantum gates.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within both the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, accounting for the comprehensive jellium potential consisting of electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions. The findings support that the composite fermions wavefunction outperforms the Laughlin wavefunction in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes as the number of electrons increases.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modeling contact issues with imperfect situations, we consider the boundary contact problem of the Stokes equations. A linear and quadratic existence and uniqueness proof is provided for a specific semicoercive variational inequality, which accounts for a mixed type condition on the contact boundary. Here, we derive and demonstrate the convergence of the mixed finite element method for this inequality, utilizing inf-sup stability and the discrete Aubin- Lions theorem.

Recent discoveries of outflows in star-forming galaxies are transforming our understanding of how star formation is regulated and the evolution of galaxies. Our research focuses on a starbursting disk, UGC 10109, where we examined how outflows are generated and the impact they have on the galaxy. Using data from radio and gamma-ray wavelengths, as well as optical and near-infrared observations, we identified a large outflow in the galaxy, where the gas is heated to high temperatures and the gas is moving at significant speeds. Our findings suggest that the outflow is regulated by star formation, where the gas is losing its gas and energy, and the gas is moving at the rate of the gas's energy output. The outflow in the galaxy is responsible for the gas's energy loss, and the gas is moving at the rate of the gas's energy output. The implications of this result are significant, as it suggests that the outflow in star-forming galaxies is responsible for the gas's energy loss, and the gas is moving at the rate of the gas's energy output.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. As the number of participating particles increased, the initial $v_3$ decreased, leading to corresponding reductions in $v_3$ of the most energetic particles. In contrast, the final $v_3$ of midrapidity charged particles exhibited a decrease with increasing centrality, mirroring the observed pattern from the STAR collaboration.

We propose a novel robotic architecture called Synchronous Robotic Framework (SRF), which employs distributed processing to synchronize real-time data from multiple robotic sensors in a coherent manner. Our framework is illustrated by a detailed description of a visual-inertial sensor fusion system, which utilizes the MIT Shark inertial measurement unit and a Logitech C920 camera. The SRF architecture is implemented using Python software, built upon the ROS (Robot Operating System) framework, and demonstrates the feasibility of real-time data synchronization with a custom data stream manager, visualized through The GDB (Graphical Debugging and Visualization) tool. This manager is constructed using HTTP requests and JSON data, enabling real-time data processing and state monitoring. Our distributed data processing system is made possible through HTTP/2 and JSON data, enabling real-time data synchronization with The GDB tool for debugging and state monitoring. This paper also provides insights into performance optimization, including data compression, data type conversion, and hardware-based data transmission.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation has proven highly successful.
However, the network architecture and training method are often treated as separate
decisions, with the latter receiving less attention. This work challenges the
conventional approach of using ImageNet as a standard pre-training dataset.
Instead, we propose integrating Monocular Depth Estimation as part of the pre-training
process, leveraging additional spatial context. By evaluating the impact of the
chosen architecture, we also conduct a comprehensive analysis of various training
configurations, comparing them to a baseline dataset. Our findings reveal that
incorporating Monocular Depth Estimation significantly improves performance, with
the specific results varying depending on the network used. Notably, we observe a
notable difference in the optimal number of image channels for fine-tuning when using
different datasets. Our best achieved scores on the Cityscapes and ADA datasets
are 77.42 mIO and 74.96 mIO, respectively.

This research focuses on identifying the best possible Bohr radius for a specific category of functions, known as log-harmonic mappings, and more specifically for those whose starlike properties exceed a certain threshold, denoted as $C$, under the unit disk. We derive a precise Bohr radius and discover that it outperforms previous estimates made by different researchers. Moreover, due to symmetries within this function class, our findings can be seamlessly translated to other classes, including $H$-convex mappings and certain harmonic functions with specific properties.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches in identifying the optimal estimate of tau, both for fixed sample sizes and over time. Furthermore, this new technique allows for a fast computation of the significance of its correlation at a given level, with the computational cost scaling quadratically.

The number of connected devices and IoT vehicles is rapidly increasing, leading to a demand for advanced decision support systems. Edge Intelligence, a promising technology, can provide autonomous driving and decision support by integrating the edge cloud and AI technology. However, user data privacy remains a significant concern. This study proposes a Privacy-Preserving Edge Intelligence (PEFI) framework, combining AI edge clustering, a deep learning-based label encoder, and an improved Federated Learning (FL) approach. The AI edge clustering technique selects optimal locations for Edge Intelligence services, reducing communication latency, while the label encoder compresses sensitive labels, enabling accurate models while protecting privacy. The PEFY framework enhances the original FL technique by improving convergence speed and accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework, showing a 16.67% improvement in accuracy and convergence speed compared to the baseline.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant that retains its primary significance even when spaces become increasingly complex and non-fundamental. Building upon this notion, multi-dimensional versions of the Euler characteristic are introduced for multi-variable spaces, allowing its application in multi-variable contexts. A new class of functions, known as Euler characteristic surfaces, is defined, and its properties are explored. This novel framework is demonstrated by applying it to multi-variable statistical analysis, specifically through the use of Eulerscapes.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's equations with a Type II predation response, also taking into account a strong Allee effect affecting prey population growth. We build on previous studies by Sabelis-Johanssen and Kermack-Gourley and establish the stability and simplicity of this modified model through minor extensions of their approaches. Our findings include confirmation that all population densities exhibit periodic behavior, as demonstrated by a Jacobian matrix analysis near an unstable, positive equilibrium point, yielding explicit expressions for these periods. Additionally, we show that the periodic prey population exhibits an unstable 'eyebrow' pattern near the prey axial system boundary, verifying that the prey period tends towards a specific limit as the predator population significantly increases.

In 2020, Delfino, Delestre, and Gaertner introduced the facet pivot algorithm for solving linear programming (LP) problems. This algorithm achieves a significant speedup compared to traditional pivot algorithms by only considering the facet edge adjacent to an (n-1)-dimensional face of the simplex table. Although more efficient, the iteration complexity of combining the facet pivot algorithm with ellipsoidal cutting remains unconfirmed. This study aims to resolve this issue by introducing the edge pivot algorithm, which integrates the facet pivot algorithm with specific cutting techniques. This modification allows for a straightforward proof that the edge pivot algorithm guarantees polynomial time performance with at most O((mn^(7/2) log(mn)/P) log(L)/P) iterations. Consequently, when applied to an (n-dimensional) LP problem with m constraints, the edge pivot algorithm achieves an impressive at most O((mn/(n^2-P) log(L)/P) log(L)/P) iterations on a polyto/P with m facets in n-dimensional space.

We explore in an associative ring R the NK1 for Bak's unitary group U*_g and establish a symbol map to H^1 with respect to Hornbostel's exact sequence, then generalize an outcome by Rozenman for the general linear group to the U*_g case.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the form of templates that are crucial for top quark mass determination.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to deceptive attacks has been a major concern in research. Recent advances have been made, including deep learning techniques for robust face anti-spooing in diverse scenarios. However, progress in this area remains limited due to the diverse nature of deceptive faces and the challenge of developing models that can generalize across different domains. To tackle this issue, transfer learning has emerged as a viable approach, and newer methods, including vision transformers, have gained traction. A comparative study was conducted to assess the vision transformer's performance against other transformer-based techniques in the vision classification task within the context of deceptive face recognition. The results indicate that the vision transformer achieves superior performance and better generalization in the target domain, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRNL) has shown great potential for autonomous driving.
Within the autonomous driving process, DRNL can be applied in several key areas.
First, it can be used for planning the vehicle's path or lane, and then for controlling the vehicle.
Second, it can be used for positioning the vehicle.
Third, it can be used for detecting objects in the environment.
Fourth, it can be used for predicting the behavior of objects in the environment.
Finally, it can be used for controlling each component of the vehicle.
This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent advancements in DRNL applications for autonomous driving.
It summarizes various DRNL frameworks and their benefits and limitations for each layer of the autonomous driving process.
The paper also provides an overview of challenges faced in each layer, and finally, highlights future research directions.

In Evolutionary Algorithms, a process where less fit individuals are eliminated and others retained continues until the algorithm's termination, but in parallel implementations, this can result in an uneven distribution of processing times among population members, causing those with shorter evaluation times to be overrepresented in parent selection, which in turn can slow down the algorithm's convergence and reduce its overall performance. Consequently, a novel technique has been proposed, which classifies solutions based on their processing times to assign each a weight for selection, thereby minimizing the impact of evaluation time bias that often plagues asynchronous Parallel Multi-objective Evolutionary Algorithms.

The 2017 microlensing event, labeled OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, involved a planet approximately 1.2 times the size of Jupiter orbiting a low-mass star. An APOGEE analysis estimated the host star's mass to be approximately 0.33 solar masses. An analysis of the light curve, incorporating the more precise host star's mass estimate, revealed a second grazing alignment and allowed for an updated analysis of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 system, including its external lensing mass. An analysis of the host star's metallicity, combined with its mass, allowed for a low estimate of the planet mass, resulting in a planet mass of approximately 5.6 to 10.5 Earth masses. An analysis of the host star's metallicity led to an estimated formation time of approximately 8.5 billion years. An analysis of the host star's distance and the lensed star's distance allowed for an estimated distance of approximately 16.7 kiloparsecs. An analysis of the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 system using Keck/NIRC2 Adaptive Optics observations allowed for a more precise measurement of the lensed star's mass and the lensed star's mass ratio, confirming the existence of the planet. The concept of a time-periodic Hamiltonian is extended to a quasiparticle model, which captures the behavior of a frequency-modulated bosonic mode under loss conditions. By developing an expansion method at high modulation frequencies, new effective descriptions are obtained for the original dynamics, which include simplified models with shifted rotation frequencies and modified loss rates. These efficient models are shown to accurately represent key dynamical properties under specific loss rate conditions. Through numerical simulations, the effectiveness of these high-frequency models is further demonstrated by comparing their one-photon excitation probability with the original dynamics. The framework presented here may hold meaningful applications in various driven-dissipative systems that are time-modulated.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh substitution in the CePd compound have
revealed how it affects its magnetic and electronic properties. Through detailed
neutron reflectivity and small-angle neutron scattering analysis, we discovered
how spin fluctuations in Ce occur and how they are influenced by substitutional
Rh. Our data indicates that spin fluctuations in Ce occur on a length scale of
several tens of Angstroms in the bulk of the material, particularly in samples
with 0.5 to 0.7 Rh substitution, corresponding to the region where the long-range
magnetic order is lost. Our calculations of the small-angle neutron scattering
intensity suggest that the size of the objects causing the fluctuations is in the
range of several tens of Angstroms, corresponding to magnetic domains.

The peak 20 features are examined in detail, revealing a total of 27 instances out of 29 peaks observed. A total of 23 features show no background continuum emission and thus cannot provide the background's thermal state, while the remaining 4 features show non-zero continuum emission but produce an estimated thermal state above 100 K. A total of 170 pc is estimated for the optical depth of the 20 features using the thermal state and HI column density observed. We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By adapting the existing knowledge about beta-transformations and Fagella's theory on beta-transformations with holes, we show that a specific intermediate beta-transformation is conjugate to a particular beta-transformation that includes a small hole near zero.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing a vast dataset of 8 femtobarns of pp collision data collected at 7 and 13 TeV with the LHCb detector, researchers reconstructed approximately 47,000 exclusive JPsipi+pi- decays of Bs mesons. Through a maximum likelihood analysis, researchers measured phi_s as 0.04 plus or minus 0.12, combined with a direct CP-violating contribution, yielding a result of phi_s = -0.06 plus or minus 0.14 where the second uncertainty arises from systematic errors. This finding aligns with the Standard Model prediction, which anticipates a small phi_s value.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel at domain-specific tasks, but their capacity to operate across diverse domains remains limited. In this research, various domain adaptation methods are tested on two distinct tasks: morphological image classification and synthesis of facial expressions. We examine a wide array of techniques involving different pairs of source and target domains, thereby determining the efficacy and versatility of each domain adaptation method. Our findings indicate that modern self-supervised methods outperform older approaches in terms of flexibility and effectiveness.

In finite fields, specific types of points called arcs are considered. An arc is a set of points where the line connecting any two points does not intersect the arc until it reaches a second arc point. We're concerned with maximal arcs specifically. A maximal arc, as defined by Sarazin, is an arc that can't be extended by adding a single point from the field. We're interested in their occurrence frequency, particularly in the F_q^2 plane where q is a power of 2. We've developed a general technique to calculate the number of maximal arcs of length l in F_q^2. As an initial finding, it turns out that in the F_q^2 plane where q is greater than 2, there are no maximal arcs of length l when l is greater than sqrt(q). Our approach is to convert the arc count issue into a calculation involving certain type sums.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it's visually represented by illustrating the triangles for the case when $n$ equals $6$.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), their complex and opaque nature hinders understanding of their behavior. While some GNN explainers have been proposed, they have limitations in providing clear and general explanations. This paper addresses this issue by proposing an explainer specifically designed for GNNs, capable of explaining the results with a parametric model. Our approach, named PGNN, utilizes the variational auto-encoder framework to analyze node and edge attributes to generate explanatory variational parameters, which can be further examined for a deeper understanding of GNN behavior. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of PGNN in generating meaningful explanations.

The dynamics within galaxy clusters are significantly influenced by their inherent
irregularities and asymmetrical structures, which can impact the formation of stars,
gas cooling, and overall evolution. To better understand these phenomena, researchers
must analyze and compare the morphological characteristics of numerous clusters. A
notable case in point is the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster, which exhibits unusual,
asymmetric features in its X-ray light, a phenomenon attributed to past subcluster
collisions. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers examined the cluster's
properties using Chandra X-ray and VLA radio telescope data. The analysis revealed
a complex web of radio filaments and hotspots, likely caused by the ejection of radio
energy from the central galaxy's magnetic fields interacting with shock waves.
Moreover, the presence of irregular shapes and asymmetrical structures in both the
X-ray and radio emissions suggest that the RXCJ0232.2-4420 cluster has undergone
extensive substructure activity, further confirmed by statistical measurements and
irregularity maps. The findings point towards ongoing, complex evolution within the
cluster, highlighting the need for further observation and theoretical advancements
to gain a deeper understanding of such phenomena.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel recurrent neural network designed to tackle sequence modeling's hardest problems, has shown promising results. A key limitation of the LMU, however, lies in its prolonged training time. To address this issue, we provide an in-depth explanation of LMU's structure and offer a novel and straightforward method for parallelizing LMU's inference and learning processes. Our approach involves explicitly mapping LMU's hidden state gradients with respect to its parameters onto batches, and shows that the data parallelization strategy can significantly reduce training time. Experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets confirm that the generalized algorithm can expedite LMU's training process, without relying on any special structural modifications. These results are then used to facilitate training a three-layer LMU on the ImageNet-1K dataset in 1.5 days, utilizing 4080 NVIDIA GPUs.

I've been wondering for 20 years whether we're on the verge of a major discovery at the LHC, or if these weakly interacting particles simply don't exist. I've decided to write this review, which could serve as an introduction to feebley interacting phenomena for new theorists, or as an old reminder for those of us who've been in the hunt for decades. The term WIMPs primarily refers to dark matter candidates that are neither baryonic nor charged. The concept of WIMPs emerged in the 1980s as a natural consequence of particle physics theories that initially had no intention of explaining dark matter. The primary models considered today are WIMPs and axions. Axions, which were first proposed in the early 1980s, have become one of the leading candidates for dark matter in recent years, with the search for them being one of the most active areas of particle physics research. The search for axions has been particularly challenging, but recent experiments have been incredibly sensitive, potentially on the brink of a major discovery. Language is a complex system that involves multiple factors such as language acquisition, the dynamic movement of people, and language changes over time. Researchers have used simplified models to study language development, including the naming game, which helps explain how language can become organized. By adding a time limit to this model and allowing people to move randomly, scientists have discovered that language can naturally develop a consistent structure without outside influence. This effect is even stronger when people move around more, and the end result is a language system that is similar to real-world languages. This research provides valuable insights into how language can develop on its own.

PINN algorithms have achieved great potential in solving various PDE-based problems, demonstrating their effectiveness in addressing both linear and non-linear equations. Despite these advancements, several issues remain, particularly when dealing with non-linear problems due to their biases toward learning linear relationships. To counteract these limitations, researchers have proposed the addition of momentum terms within the network's loss function. Our study delves into the impact of momentum terms in PINN algorithms, starting with an examination of the theoretical properties of generalization in the context of the heat equation. Our research finds that introducing momentum terms within the network's loss function can decrease the experimental bias, particularly when considering high-frequency components. Moreover, by comparing PINN with momentum terms to traditional neural networks, we have discovered that adding momentum terms can diminish the spectral bias of the network, thereby decreasing the gap in the loss function between high- and low-frequency components. Our study further demonstrates the effectiveness of PINN with momentum terms in complex applications, utilizing a steady-state heat equation solved on a square domain.

We examine a two-wave system in the domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, where $\Omega$ has a smooth boundary $\Gamma$, and at least one of the waves experiences Kelvin-Voigt damping, with damping, for a portion $\Gamma_0$ of the boundary $\Gamma$, varying from perfectly dissipative, through locally, to fully non-dissipative.  2D and 3D geometric conditions are imposed for the perfect dissipation case to occur and to occur strongly.  2D geometric conditions are imposed for a system that does not experience perfect dissipation, but experiences strong dissipation, to occur and for a pair of waves with different propagation speeds.  3D geometric conditions are imposed for a system that does not experience perfect dissipation, but experiences strong dissipation, to occur for a pair of waves with the same or different propagation speeds.  2D geometric conditions are imposed for our geometric condition $\Gamma_0$ to occur and for a pair of waves with different propagation speeds.  3D geometric conditions are imposed for our geometric condition $\Gamma_0$ to occur for a pair of waves with the same or different propagation speeds.

Recent advances in reinforcement learning have produced highly effective model-based techniques that can learn complex environments with improved sample efficiency. However, these approaches often struggle to reveal the underlying relationships between states, actions, and rewards in a way that's easily understood by humans. To address this limitation, we're building on a previously developed method that used inductive logic programming to derive the reasons an agent takes certain actions. We extend this work by incorporating the ability to learn the relationships between rewards and the rewards themselves, enabling the system to tackle problems with multiple rewards. Moreover, we introduce the use of tree-based logic programming, which significantly speeds up the process of finding the optimal policy and generates more interpretable results. Through extensive experimentation involving both simulated and real-world challenges, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in generating and learning the reasons behind agent actions, as well as deriving the relationships within those explanations, which has been validated using explanation-based learning.

We've developed an approach for achieving optical nonreciprocity through the process of quantum squeezing, relying solely on the disordered phase that arises from optical parametric amplification. By employing a weak amplifying phase, we've demonstrated that significant nonreciprocal effects can emerge when a system is closely approached to its disordered state, allowing for a significant enhancement in the anti-Cherenkov effect, which could be as high as ten times its suppressed form. Furthermore, our research shows that an optimally chosen pump frequency can lead to over tenfold improvement in a nonreciprocal device's sensitivity to weak probe signals compared to its response to strong coherent ones.

We establish a sum-of-translates variant of the Fengent problem, and for function spaces in 1D and 2D, we demonstrate how to compute a precise solution to this variant along with relevant optimality criteria. Our study delves into the properties of a novel function norm, which we call the Fenton norm, that's derived from the fundamental solution of the 1D wave equation, in the context of the real and complex number systems, and we extend our work to a broader class of hyperbolic fundamental solutions, including those linked to wave equations in 2D and Schrödinger equations, which may be relevant in quantum mechanics. Additionally, we investigate connections to neural networks and relevant function spaces like Besov spaces and Bessel potential spaces. As a side note, we prove a new characterization of a particular function norm, which we call the Bessel potential norm.

The CRESST experiment, a direct dark matter search, has achieved 24 months of data collection and used $^6$Li-doped TeO$_2$ detectors to examine spin-dependent interactions with gluons and axial-vector couplings, particularly targeting light dark matter particles weighing less than 0.5 GeV/$c^2$. An innovative analysis technique was implemented to assess the reliability of background rejection methods before reporting results, and background-rejected data from 24 months of observation were utilized for these analyses. Based on 6-kGg-day detector mass, no interactions were detected, allowing comparison with previous studies on $^{100}$Sn and $^{129}$I. Specifically, our study places the most stringent bounds to date on light dark matter interactions involving axial coupling with up quarks through SI interactions mediated by Higgs bosons, particularly below 0.1 GeV masses, and we also report new limits on interactions involving ADPs.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image and a motion model from a single observed image. This problem is challenging due to ill-posedness and non-convex optimization difficulties. Successful deblurring relies heavily on the utilization of image priors that impose smoothness. In this research, we formulate the blurred image as a convolution of two latent variables: the latent image and a kernel representing the blur. The blur is further assumed to be a convolution of the scene's point spread function and the motion kernel. We develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm to iteratively solve the deblurring and demosaicking process. Additionally, we incorporate a new flexible and adaptive method to estimate the kernel and its correlation with the scene. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to recover high-quality images from low-resolution inputs, outperforming existing methods.

This paper introduces a new concept, called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with coefficients, and demonstrates its connection to bi-coalgebra-cocommutative coalgebra structures on Hopf-module cocommutative coalgebras. Additionally, we relate this idea to the established theories of bi-Hopf and associative BiHom-coalgebra systems. Specifically, we define an innovative framework, called Nonhomogeneous BiHopf-Racah-coalgebra family (or BNHC family for short), which integrates existing co algebra-coalgebra theories, and contains important special cases such as Hopf-coalgebra coquasitriple co algebras and Yang-Baxter-coalgebra coquasitriple co algebras. This new framework is characterized by a specific equation: (R1 ⊗ R1 ⊗ Id)(Ω(R1) ⊗ Ω(R2)) + (Id ⊗ R2 ⊗ R2)(Ω(R2) ⊗ Ω(R1)) = 0. This equation serves as a foundational cornerstone for co algebra-coalgebra co quasi-invariant forms. As an application of this theory, we introduce a novel class of objects, called Pair of Nonhomogeneous Yang-Baxter-co-Hopf systems, which encompasses a significant co Hopf system, namely the pair (R1, R2) of bi-Hopf-coalgebra-coquasi-invariant forms.

Formal verification offers a rigorous framework for ensuring software reliability, but it remains a challenging task due to its complex and constrained syntax. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach called Natural Hoare Logic (NHL), which leverages an enhanced version of the Hoare logic to extract meaning from informal program descriptions written in everyday language. This method employs a syntax-tomantics procedure to translate informal program specifications into formal assertion formulas, thus enabling traditional Hoare logic-based verification methods to be applied. Furthermore, the current study expands upon the NHL framework to include the detection of infinite loops in programs and provides a definition of software outputs using predicates, thus facilitating the formal verification of recursive programs. The NVIDIA CUDA kernel sort, a practical case study, is employed to demonstrate the practical applicability of the NHL framework in real-world software verification.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchain systems, to operate correctly. The Canopus algorithm has been developed as an efficient consensus mechanism for blockchain systems, offering improved performance and reduced resource consumption compared to traditional Byzantine tolerance algorithms. However, Canopus has a limitation in handling node failures. The RCanopus algorithm builds upon Canopus to detect failures and initiate the failure of unreliable nodes, offering improved reliability and scalability. Notably, in the event of a node failure, RCanopus can achieve a higher overall throughput compared to other reliable consensus algorithms, and outperforms Canopus by 50% in terms of overall resource consumption. The experimental setup utilized Apache Cassandra as a distributed database to compare the performance of RCanopus with other existing consensus algorithms, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency as a reliable consensus mechanism.

Our research involves using computer simulations to explore the bending properties of lipid bilayers containing cholesterol. We utilized Monte Carlo modeling with simplified representations of chiral lipids to generate ensembles and calculated the statistical operator representing bending modulus. The simulation's findings align with existing experimental data, demonstrating the validity of this approach. We discovered that the binary lipid system exhibits a transition temperature in the temperature range of 300-350 K and observed an inverse relationship between bending modulus and the temperature at which it occurs. Notably, our research indicates increased flexibility in lipid bilayers containing cholesterol compared to cholesterol-free lipids in the same environment.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model derived from the ADM Hamiltonian, focusing on the Lorentzian signature case, which includes solutions for both open and closed universes. By solving the resulting differential equations, we generate universe evolution graphs and compare them to classical solutions. We discover a critical difference: the quantum models maintain a finite maximum radius for closed universes, in stark contrast to their classical counterparts, where radii can expand indefinitely. This distinct characteristic sets the quantum models apart from their classical predecessors.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a 
wide energy range from 8.0 to 30.5 EeV. This comprehensive dataset, made 
available for further research, includes observations made during the first 
phase of the augmented surface array phase.

Incorporating deep object detectors into safety-critical applications requires assessing their uncertainty to determine their reliability. Although uncertainty estimation has been widely applied to regression and semantic segmentation tasks, its implementation in object detection remains limited. This study proposes a Bayesian approach for providing uncertainty estimates in object detection, adapting Monte Carlo Dropout to object detectors and incorporating uncertainty estimation into the loss function to stabilize training. Our method effectively produces uncertainty estimates that, when combined with random sampling, accurately reflect the uncertainty of an object detector's output, outperforming previous methods in terms of calibration, especially for rare event calibration.

The practical application of traffic forecasting in transportation is a widely recognized concept that can be effectively used for a range of purposes. However, forecasting a continuous function, like traffic on highways, is a more complex challenge. To address this challenge, the traffic forecast optimization problem has been broken down into two manageable tasks: predicting discrete states of traffic patterns and counting the durations of these states. To achieve this, a novel approach called Traffic Moving Snippets (TMSn) was developed, adapting it from the Traffic Moving Snapshot (TMS) framework. The key difference lies in TMSn's focus on classifying traffic patterns as sequences of evolving frames, or 'words', which are then used to predict future frames.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been applied to the study of Gray categories. This research delves into the connection between rewriting and Gray categories, focusing on the development of a rewriting algorithm for matrices representing 2-cells in free 2-categories. It utilizes this algorithm to give a rewriting-based proof of the coherence theorem for braided categories. Furthermore, the algorithm is employed in reconstructing Gray's characterization of strictified 2-categories and providing a framework for testing equivalence in 2-categories through its confluence.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images is a crucial component in diagnosing Alzheimer's and epilepsy. Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks, have demonstrated significant potential in this application. We addressed several challenges associated with epilepsy and neurodegenerative disease studies by developing an advanced 3D U-Net architecture and training it on the largest hippocampus training datasets available. We validated our approach by achieving a high performance on challenging datasets, including those with multiple convolutional neural networks and state-of-the-art metrics.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through analysis with single, two, and many particles, and by introducing transversal modes, we uncover the control of pairwise interactions relies on external classical information, and the observed pair separation isn't genuinely robust but modifiable by introducing a mode orthogonal to the forward path direction.

Our research focuses on determining the radiation danger for future astronauts in low Earth orbit, using a modified version of the GEANT4 simulation tool. This simulation, called GEANT4-LEO, models the effects of different types of cosmic rays, including protons, on humans in low Earth orbit. As these high-energy particles collide with aluminum structures, they fragment and create heavier ions, such as iron, which then continue to interact and create even smaller particles, like helium. 

In this simulation, we used GEANT4's default settings to simulate the production of ions and found that our model accurately predicts the risks associated with space radiation, as it replicates data obtained from existing measurements. 

We found that high-energy particles, such as silicon, increase the risk of radiation damage to humans in low Earth orbit, and that our model can help us understand the potential dangers for future astronauts. 

To conduct this simulation, we used a supercomputer with a lot of processing power to simulate a lot of particles, and we found that our model can help us predict the radiation danger for future missions. 

We found that the simulation accurately predicts the risks associated with space radiation, and that our model can help us design safer spaceships and better shielding for future missions. 

Overall, our model can help us understand the potential dangers for future missions and help us design safer spaceships and better shielding for future missions.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, but it's rarely considered a priority during their design. This research demonstrates the expressivity constraint of graph neural networks can be effectively addressed by two key strategies: globally shrinking the model's skeleton and reconfiguring its local connections. Various empirical experiments have confirmed the proposed design philosophy significantly enhances the performance of GNNs, offering valuable insights for the architecture development of deep graph neural networks. Additionally, source codes are available at https://github.com/PhoEne/PyGEESS.

To enhance robustness in low-rank matrix completion under privacy constraints, we propose a novel differential privacy strategy, a 'truncated' mechanism inspired by the Huber loss function, and prove its effectiveness by demonstrating its distance to the original mechanism within a $\epsilon'$-differential privacy framework. We also suggest a corresponding algorithm and demonstrate its superiority in numerical tests.

We propose a novel approach to interstellar dust modeling, which involves combining large-scale observations and high-resolution spectroscopy to characterize the physical and chemical properties of the diffuse interstellar medium.  We introduce a two-component dust model comprising a granular silicate and carbonaceous grain component referred to as astrodust, along with a PAH component.  The astrodust is represented by irregularly shaped, non-crystalline grains of silica, silicate, carbon, and graphite, with sizes ranging from 0.1 to 100 nanometers.  The PAH component is comprised of complex aromatic hydrocarbons, which are essential to accurately reproduce the ultraviolet and optical polarization caused by interstellar dust.  We evaluate our model against the far-ultraviolet extinction in the Milky Way and M31 galaxies, as well as the ultraviolet and optical polarization levels, and find that it accurately matches the observed data.  Furthermore, our model reproduces the ultraviolet and optical starlight polarization and the ultraviolet and optical extinction, with minor discrepancies in the ultraviolet region.  We compare our model to the ultraviolet extinction measurements from four space missions, and our results align with the data from the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Telescope, the Cosmic Background Explorer, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the Future EUV Space Telescope.  We also successfully match the ultraviolet and optical polarization levels and the ultraviolet and optical extinction, with minor discrepancies in the ultraviolet

Research on protoplanetary disk evolution and planetary formation has been significantly advanced by the discovery of CIDA 1, a low-mass star hosting a massive disk featuring a distinct gap. Our findings reveal that CIDA 1, previously thought to be a massive disk around a low-mass star, actually has a mass comparable to solar-mass stars with smaller disks. Furthermore, our research indicates that the gap in CIDA 1's disk is likely not due to viscosity but rather to the gravitational influence of a massive planet. Using radiative transfer models, our analysis shows that the dust in CIDA 1's disk is predominantly composed of giant ring structures located at approximately 10-15 astronomical units. Furthermore, our findings suggest the presence of a massive planet located at around 22-28 astronomical units, which is responsible for shaping the gap. This planet could be responsible for the observed gap and its location aligns with theoretical expectations for planet formation in low-mass stars.

Consider the games Lights Out and Lights Out Pro, both played on a graph with nodes that can be in one of two states: on or off. Initially, all nodes are on, and at each turn, pressing a node flips its own state and the states of its adjacent nodes. Although Light Out is simpler, it cannot be played on graphs with odd cycles, whereas Lights Out Pro has no such limitation. We developed a measure of difficulty for graphs in Lights Out Pro, determining the minimum number of clicks required to solve them, and found that this difficulty measure is symmetric. Specifically, if a graph's difficulty measure is m, then its complement's difficulty measure plus original graph's difficulty measure equals the total number of nodes in the graph times m.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining image enhancement and variant energy minimization. Addressing image degeneration issues such as blur and noise, we integrate these processes to improve segmentation accuracy. Our approach addresses color image segmentation by proposing the Binary Total Variation with Poisson Denoising model, and Gray Image Segmentation with Outlier Image Degradation Binary Total Variation model. Additionally, we extend these models to handle chromatic aberration aberration aberration failures. The proposed models effectively restore blurred and noisy images, demonstrating robust segmentation capabilities even under severe chromatic aberrations. Experimental results highlight the superior segmentation performance and anti-degeneration abilities of our approach.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis terminates, and the downward phase refines the approximations to improve accuracy. A new approach called Abstract Counterexample Refinement (ACR) separates these phases by generating precise, non-approximated traces directly from the initial analysis, and then refining them separately based on feasibility and precision. This innovation offers several potential benefits over traditional methods.

A hermitian topology underpins physical phenomena, yet its application to phonons in solids is hindered by the non-hermitian nature of coupled phonon-phonon-electron systems. We demonstrate that hermitian phonon bands can emerge in this context when there is strong light absorption, due to decoupling electron-phonon interactions from phonon dynamics. This method allows for topological phonon modes at various frequencies, which can potentially be used for multiple purposes. However, their detection and utilization are hindered when electrons participate in phonon scattering. This limitation can be overcome in insulators at low temperatures or in metals with high resistance, enabling the research and application of topological phonons. Our proposed methodology thus provides a general framework for modeling a non-hermitian system as an optical probe of topological phonons.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based algorithms, despite the high computational costs and inefficiencies associated with them.  A novel approach to addressing this challenge involves avoiding direct outlier detection by leveraging proximity graphs, where distance computations rely solely on nearest neighbor relationships rather than pairwise comparisons.  This paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of using proximity graphs to expedite outlier detection in general metric spaces, proposing an innovative graph construction method combining Voronoi and Delaunay constructions.  Furthermore, a novel technique for efficiently traversing proximity graphs is introduced, enhancing the overall detection process.  Through thorough experimentation, the proposed method demonstrates significant speedups over traditional techniques based on random sampling and underpins a novel Delaunay-based proximity graph approach, yielding speedups of up to 2 orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art outlier detection methods.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied at the boundary. When an atom in its excited state moves perpendicular to the mirror, it undergoes acceleration-induced stimulation to lose energy, causing emission of a photon, whereas emission of photons from an atom in its ground state or excited energy levels was not observed. Conversely, when the atom moves parallel to the surface, it experiences stimulation to become excited or lose energy, resulting in photon emission. When in its excited state, the mirror causes atoms to stimulate energy loss through both static emission and Zeeman shifts in frequency due to the influence of the mirror, as well as linear and quadratic Doppler shifts in frequency due to the movement. When the atom is in its ground state, only static emission and Zeeman shifts in frequency were found to occur, but not the latter two phenomena. Furthermore, it was discovered that the atom's velocity leads to a reverse flow of energy being absorbed from the vacuum due to emission not occurring under certain conditions. When the atom is excited, it will normally emit a photon with energy increased in value due to the influence of the mirror, causing the photon to move away from the surface, whereas the reverse scenario occurs when the atom moves,

In many applications using graph representations, such as graph classification, there's a need to ensure fair outcomes, especially when making predictions on nodes and their connections. To address this issue, we've developed a framework for promoting fairness between neighboring nodes within a graph, which builds upon mutual information theory. Our approach first extends the concept of localized data fairness from traditional machine learning to graph classification, then generalizes it across different graph representation techniques, including structural, non-structural, and hybrid methods. We provide theoretical justification for these generalizations and evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework through extensive experiments.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in determining the approximate analytical solutions of related non-linear differential equations. We examine the accuracy of these methods by comparing them to kinetic parameters derived from NMR titration data of enzymes. Additionally, we consider the role of the quasi-steady-state assumption in enzyme reaction models and assess its applicability based on the relative concentrations of enzymes and substrates.

A search was conducted to detect supersymmetry produced in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, focusing on patterns with overlapping jets and unmeasured momentum. Using data from the CMS experiment with 36.12 inverse femtobarns of recorded events, researchers analyzed potential signs of supersymmetry by searching for pairs of photons, leptons, or at no isolated leptons, in conjunction with significant amounts of jet and unmeasured momentum. Analyzing different mass ranges of colored particles, researchers established upper limits on their relative production rates for simplified models of compressed or split supersymmetry, where the production of colored particles is related to the tree-level production of squarks and gluinos. In the split-susym model, limits were set for the mass range of 1.2 to 6 TeV for neutralinos of odd spin.

Two proposed expectation-finishing criteria assess rational expectation financial bubbles: one examines the diminishing probability of a financial asset's continued existence into the future, while the other evaluates the anticipated duration of a financial asset's continued existence. In this study, the expectations-finishing criteria are explored through the lens of a particular stochastic process that naturally models and models the continuous, organized, and predictable patterns of various financial assets. Our analysis demonstrates that both criteria are equivalent and can be characterized by the start and exponent of the probability density function of a financial asset's termination, which corresponds to the mean-reverting and termination-related parameters of the process. The stochastic process's mean-reverting parameter influences the probability density function's shape, which in turn determines the validity and applicability of both diagnostics for different types of financial assets. The first diagnostic is generally applicable to all types of financial assets, as long as the probability density function is unimodal, whereas the second diagnostic is generally applicable to assets with termination probabilities that are log-concave. The paper also includes the analysis of several financial asset examples.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either constant driving forces or time-vareing periodic movements. 
Calculations of position, momentum, and energy along with the quantum action were carried out. 
A two-dimensional simulation was performed on an Apple M1 Pro chip using the Mac operating system. 
The short-time propagator formula was represented as a series of discrete time-steps known as a path integral. 
By breaking down the action into its constituent parts - kinetic and potential terms - a path was traced through the quantum oscillator's configurations. 
By applying the trapezoidal rule formula and approximating the action at each iteration, a path was traced through the quantum oscillator's configurations. 
By applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, upper and lower bounds were established for the oscillator's energy levels, confirming the convergence of the path integral. 
By applying the arithmetic and geometric means, a path was traced through the quantum oscillator's configurations.

Recent research has shown that combining item-based and sentiment-aware techniques can significantly enhance recommender systems, as user reviews contain valuable insights into an item. However, existing methods have significant limitations, such as treating all reviews equally and ignoring user individuality. To address these issues, we have developed a Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion (SIFN) model for review-based item recommendation. This model generates a dynamic, context-dependent embedding vector for each item by integrating multiple abstract representations, including coarse-grained and fine-grained vectors, and uses a Sentiment-aware Review (SR) network to learn review embeddings based on individual sentiment scores and abstract topics. The interaction between item and review embeddings, along with user and location context, is then leveraged in our model to produce accurate and effective recommendations. Experimental results on three real-world datasets confirm that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and comprehensiveness.

Developing machine translation models that can handle code-switched texts is particularly challenging due to the lack of sufficient parallel data. This difficulty is primarily attributed to difficulties in identifying the content words within the text and determining their meanings. Cross-lingual word embeddings have been shown to be effective in determining word meanings, especially in data-rich languages. This paper explores the effectiveness of Arabic pre-trained and cross-lingual model word embeddings for identifying the contents of the words in code-switched texts. We propose an approach that utilizes cross-lingual embeddings to perform data augmentation by replacing Arabic words in the content-rich texts with English words. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method on the content-rich and code-switched portions of the machine translation system. The results demonstrate that incorporating the content-rich texts with augmented content from our strategy improves the performance of the machine translation system, especially on the data-rich portion.
