A new research area called RGMGRF has recently emerged, which researchers 
have been using to study the properties of manifolds of GRFs. 
In this research, we focus on the geodesic curves in manifolds of GRFs, which researchers 
have been using to analyze the properties of these curves and develop novel algorithms. 
We develop two techniques for computing the length of geodesic curves in manifolds of GRFs, 
which researchers have been using to analyze the properties of these curves and design 
efficient algorithms. 
In addition, we propose a novel algorithm for computing the exponential map 
of GRF manifolds using the RGMGRF framework, which researchers have been using to analyze 
the properties of these curves and develop novel techniques. 
Our research presents a comprehensive analysis of the properties of GRF manifolds, 
which researchers have been using to analyze the properties of these curves 
and design efficient algorithms.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we show that the $L$-function $L(F, \chi, s)$ has finite denominators at all special values, especially for $s=n+1$. In addition, we establish lower bounds for the growth of these bounded denominators and prove a related result for L-functions linked to automorphic representations of $GL_n$.

In a narrow armchair graphene nanoribbon with a consistent width of one nanometer and subjected to a magnetic field perpendicular to it, we have explored spin-dependent transport properties when contacts are attached. Our study reveals spin filtering and remarkable conductance fluctuations triggered by the interference of electron waves. These effects vary significantly with the size of the nanoribbon due to its width. Our findings suggest the possibility of achieving spin filtering and fluctuations within nanostructures that are visible to the naked eye.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of length k for all possible k values between 3 and n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that if a connected graph on n vertices has an independence number alpha(G) that is less than n/3, then it must contain all cycles. Researchers have since sought to find the minimum independence number required for a pancyclic graph. Asgharian, Kravitz, and Li determined the exact minimum for n being at least 100, finding that a graph is pancyclic when its independence number is at most 3n/10 - O(1). This paper further reduces the lower bound from 3n/10 to 2n/5 - O(1), matching the known example.

The movement of particles in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions has been studied in the context of heavy-ion collisions. Directed flow ($p_t$ dependence of $v_1$) measurements have been performed for rho mesons and photons in 201, 2012, and 2016 collisions between gold-gold, zirconium-zirconium, and oxygen-oxygen systems. Comparisons of these results reveal significant zirconium-gold differences in zirconium-zirconium and gold-gold collisions at lower energies, whereas similar values were obtained for gold-gold and oxygen-oxygen collisions. In contrast, similar results were obtained in ruthenium-ruthenium and zirconium-zirconium collisions. These differences suggest a zirconium's role in shaping proton momentum at lower energies, whereas similar values were obtained for ruthenium and zirconium. Additionally, similar values were obtained for directed flow between gold-gold and oxygen-oxygen collisions at a lower energy, whereas similar values were obtained between ruthenium-ruthenium and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a lower energy. Similar values were obtained between directed flow between isospin systems at a lower energy, whereas similar values were obtained between isospin systems at a lower energy. These differences suggest that nucleon interactions with mesons and photons at a lower energy are influenced by isospin,

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex nonlinear dynamical systems by converting them into a simplified linear system for analysis. This approach uses an intermediate data transformation step to define a spectral problem that can be bypassed when using a conventional Koopman method. In this study, we derive a new, efficient method that dynamically increases model complexity during this transformation step. By adapting the grid size and complexity based on available data, this approach optimizes computational resources. In addition, we develop a computational framework that significantly reduces the computational burden. Our analysis shows that this method is effective across various computational domains, including a range of scientific models from simple systems to complex three-dimensional domain problems.

This review provides an overview of key findings for the implementation of the ECS method in a range of scenarios involving DC and time-dependent fields. These situations include photoionization processes for atoms in a DC field, ionization of molecules along various axes, charge exchange reactions between ions, the separation of ion pairs in molecular ions under the influence of a DC field, the interaction of atoms under the influence of a DC laser pulse, and the photoionization properties of molecules.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely employed solution for urban air-emission estimation, despite some versions lacking guarantees of convergence and for problems where it finds no solution. This research investigates the mathematical underpinnings of the algorithm and its convergence behavior. When it doesn't converge, it may approach a target that doesn't correspond to a well-defined problem solution. We present mathematical criteria determining whether such non-convergent behavior occurs, which may result in using values beyond a sensible range for practical applications such as emission inventory calculations.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC has recorded data of 26.9 fb$^{-1}$ in 5.02 TeV $pp$ collisions, which are used to determine the$t\bar{t}$ production cross-section in different decay channels, including one-tau and two-tau final states and isolated leptons. The measured $t\bar{t}$ cross-sections align with the predictions made by the NLO-PQCD model in good agreement with the predictions made by the LHCBJ fixed-order and parton-shower models. The uncertainty in the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurement is dominated by the statistical error in the data.

Key factors that cause the dynamics of quantum systems to become localized 
are the characteristics of the system itself, external disorder, and its interaction 
with a complex surroundings, such as a thermal bath. In this paper, the authors 
investigate the effects of a quantum system's interaction with a model thermal bath 
consisting of a grid of harmonic oscillators driven by a central force. The authors 
apply the participation ratio to study the dynamics of the system's state and 
observe the emergence of transient dynamics characterized by delocalization and 
subsequent localization. The researchers' analysis reveals that while pure 
unitary evolution leads to transient delocalization, adding a weak coupling 
resulting in non-markovian dynamics causes the quantum coherence to diminish and 
localize the quantum state, thus suppressing the delocalization effect. The team 
also studies the effects of disorder and driving force on the thermal state of 
the system and observes the emergence of the many-body localized phase under 
specific conditions.

The conditions on $A, B, p,$ and $\alpha,$ where $-1 \leq A, B \leq 1$ and $0 \leq \alpha < 1,$ are determined to guarantee that $f(z)$ belongs to the class $I_{p}^{1}(B, A, \alpha)$ for $f(z)=z g_{p-1}(z)$. Also, the conditions for $f(z)$ to belong to the classes $I_{p}^{1}(0, 1, \alpha)$ and $I_{\infty}^{1}(1, 1, \alpha)$ are identified as the discussed problems are novel. These problems have been solved using two methods: the subordination approach and the algebraic form of subordination.

Urban settings drive economic and social growth, yet understanding daily human movement is a complex challenge. Traditional data sources such as transportation cards and mobile location data merely reveal movement between locations but fall short in providing a detailed understanding of urban patterns. However, dynamic social influence patterns, captured through in-facetwork analysis, can accurately reflect social and economic processes. We have developed the T- Facet methodology and applied it to "Facetlets" - dynamic components of public discourse networks - to measure changes in urban patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic. By analyzing Facetlets from The Washington Post's discussion forum, we found significant shifts in urban patterns due to the pandemic. Moreover, the pandemic led to changes in public discourse networks, revealing a decline in support for diversity and inclusivity values among urban users compared to pre-pandemic periods.

This paper delves into the development of nonlinear field-split preconditioners for efficient approximation of complex two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. By incorporating parameters that vary across different parts of the medium, we examine the impact of scatter in these parameters on field-split approaches. Our study reveals that field-split Newton-type algorithms, field-split implicit methods, and implicit residual preconditioned implicit methods all converge forscattered parameters, yet their convergence rates vary depending on the degree of scatter. We analyze a specific implicit residual preconditioner and develop an efficient approach to compute its nonlinear preconditioner in real-time. We also investigate how convergence is affected when using residual versus original preconditioners and how different types of convergence monitors perform across various levels of scatter in the medium. Numerical tests were conducted using realistic 3D models to assess the performance of these methods for different ranges of scatter in the medium parameters.

A key property of chemical bonds is its ability to exist in either a "handed" or opposite form, which is illustrated by the examples of right-handed and left-handed configurations. In the realm of quantum physics, there are few examples of a substance consisting solely of one type of configuration - in this case, the substance consists of either right-handed or left-handed configurations - without the presence of the opposite configuration. In the present study, we have achieved a breakthrough by demonstrating a crucial characteristic of this substance - its ability to reflect and trap light in a specific way, which allows for the creation of a stable cavity of specific chirality. Under particular conditions, the substance can trap light of the opposite configuration, which allows for the examination of its inherent properties, including its ability to emit light in a specific pattern, which could have significant implications for the development of new technologies in this field.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti-de Sitter 2-space and a semi-classical Liouville theory, with the boundary condition of the gravitational action matching the central charge $c_\texttt{t} = 1$. We find that the gravitational action with its Iyer-Wald term yields the same asymptotic behavior as the correlation functions of the Liouville theory, with the thermal partition function, 1- and 2-point functions matching the corresponding models. By incorporating the bulk operator $\Phi_\phi$ into the Liouville vertex operator $\Phi_\phi \sim e^{2\phi}$, we demonstrate that the correlation functions of 2-point functions involving bulk operators also align. This correspondence is further extended to unitary Hermitian matrix models, where the large $N$ limit's partition functions and correlation functions of the modified Hermitian matrix models, featuring an additional constant term $\frac{c_\texttt{t} N}{2}$ in the potentials, match those of the corresponding Liouville theory and Liftschitz-Gotze invariants for the correlation functions.

A spacetime distortion, often called a warp bubble, could potentially allow objects to travel faster than light by shrinking the space ahead and expanding it behind. This effect, known as warp drive, has been explored through various theoretical models. This paper investigates the conditions necessary for creating warp drive solutions involving both a perfect fluid and the effects of the cosmological constant. By analyzing these factors, the study finds that it is theoretically possible to create these solutions, but with significant challenges due to the backreaction of matter and the requirements for the matter distribution involved. This research builds upon existing literature, including Alford et al. and White paper, and considers the effects of different values of the parameter $k$ and the density $\rho_0$ of the matter distribution. While this study finds that it is theoretically feasible to create warp drive solutions under certain conditions, further research is necessary to determine their practical viability using realistic matter distributions and the effects of quantum gravity.

As urban centers around the globe expand and become increasingly reliant on digital information, a critical need arises for well-organized urban data to support informed decision-making and efficient problem-solving. Current approaches, however, face significant challenges in managing such complex datasets. To address this issue, researchers have developed a large-scale framework called GUIDES, which streamlines the process of creating detailed three-dimensional urban infrastructure models by streamlining data integration and processing. By leveraging open-source tools and comprehensive geospatial data, GUIDES enables the automatic generation of highly accurate urban models down to the individual building level. Furthermore, these models hold substantial value for a wide range of urban applications and can be applied in diverse fields such as urban planning, urban design, and public policy.

To analyze the center-of-mass motional states of a 2D lithium-7 ion crystal, composed of 14 ions between $x$-magnets, we utilized spin dephasing techniques. This analysis revealed the individual motional state distributions of each normal mode and the overall mode temperature, which can be directly correlated to the overall ion crystal temperature. This study establishes a precise relationship between spin dephasing and motional state parameters. Consequently, it enables the development of an adiabatic cooling protocol, where the mode temperature is reduced to as low as 150 microkelvin. Furthermore, by comparing our experimentally obtained cooling limits to simulations, an upper limit of $50$ nanokelvin is placed on the cooling rate. Additionally, this work sets a $50$ nanokelvin limit on the residual spin dephasing, caused by experimental imperfections, at zero motional mode temperature.

This research employs full quantum treatment to investigate the interaction between a silver nanoparticle and a molecular monolayer of benzene molecules in the context of TERS, without relying on the approximation of a continuous metal. By employing quantum simulations, researchers were able to directly trace the interaction between the benzene molecule and the silver nanoparticle's electronic states. Surprisingly, the researchers found that the effect of charge transfer between the benzene molecule and the silver nanoparticle plays a crucial role in enhancing the TERS signal and is even more significant than classically predicted. Furthermore, the quantum simulations revealed that the electromagnetic field created by the silver nanoparticle significantly deforms the molecular orbitals of the benzene molecule. The deformation leads to asymmetric orbitals, which significantly distort the molecular orbitals and shift the molecular absorption bands to lower energy frequencies. The deformation also polarizes the benzene molecule and generates a dipole that generates an asymmetric charge distribution around the molecule. Quantum simulations reveal that these asymmetric properties of molecular absorption bands are crucial in explaining the TERS signal observed in experiments.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of the nearby Coma cluster, observing its members at different times. Our focus was on detecting the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) in nearby galaxies, which remains unconfirmed despite initial millimeter-wave observations. We analyzed the frequency-dependent emission characteristics and modeled its components, including thermal dust, starlight, and free-free emission. We modeled the thermal and free-free components using galaxy templates and isolated star-forming regions. We found no significant AME emission, with a 2σ upper limit of 100 K in temperature. This sets a constraint on AME, particularly in star-forming galaxies like NGC 4486, and we discuss the implications of our results.

Ammonium sulfate exhibits a notable electric field caloric effect accompanied by an enormous entropy change, making it a fascinating system for investigation. A key aspect of this anomaly is the substantial entropy change resulting from the electric field, which surpasses that found in typical ferroelectrics by orders of magnitude. Researchers have, however, identified this unusual phenomenon as closely linked to a simultaneous rotational entropy of the molecules within the crystal, which becomes unlocked by the electric field. In this work, we confirm the presence of this rotational entropy through a combination of neutron scattering and ab initio calculations. The findings indicate that the rotation of the molecules occurs continuously, rather than gradually, as a function of temperature, as suggested by the current literature.

In reinforcement learning tasks, agents make optimal decisions by accurately weighing the significance of rewards.
However, humans frequently display inconsistent learning behaviors, which cannot be explained by standard reinforcement learning models.
This study reveals that while individuals demonstrate varied learning behaviors, they consistently prioritize rewards similarly in their brain activity.
This finding suggests that people's suboptimal decision-making strategies remain consistent throughout their lives and has implications for understanding and predicting individual decision-making behavior.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could help clarify the relationship between quantum entanglement and contextuality. By exploring an 8x8 grid model and its connection to the Witting configuration, we discovered a structural similarity between them. Building on the standard $E_8$ root system, with its 240 roots, we can find multiple 40-ray complexes, showcasing the rich mathematical underpinnings of these structures.

The continuous Fréchet distance is a widely used metric that measures the similarity between two curves, often seen in applications such as comparing motion trajectories and image shapes. This work focuses on an important computational problem called the approximate near neighbor (ANN) searching problem where the goal is to find similar instances in a dataset of curves. We first establish a fundamental lower bound on the time required to solve this problem by creating a scenario called the grid problem which has a time complexity of $\Omega(n)$. The grid problem essentially asks to detect if there are any close points on a grid of distinct colors. This problem has a time complexity of $\Omega(n)$, and by mapping it to our ANN problem, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ for any problem that seeks out its most similar instances. This lower bound is achieved by constructing an instance where all points except for the closest ones are colored in a way that forces any algorithm solving the ANN problem to spend at least $\Omega(n)$ time. We then provide matching upper bounds of $O(n)$ and $O(n/\epsilon)$, showing that our problem is as efficient as possible and cannot be made any faster.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors in quantum experiments employing probabilistic measurement models, a novel approach is introduced in this study. The method is based on Bayesian unfolding and efficiently addresses the mitigations of cross-talk, photon loss, and detector inefficiencies. Unlike earlier techniques, this approach scales linearly with the number of error types, rather than exponentially. Furthermore, by utilizing an alternating minimization strategy, the method yields optimal solutions that satisfy all noise constraints. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, the authors apply the mitigation to a five-qubit quantum query algorithm and a quantum information setup. The experimental results confirm the method's accuracy, and the simulations reveal its ability to achieve quadratic convergence and efficient convergence.

In the realm of human-robot interaction, particularly in areas like assistance, inspection, and search & rescue operations, understanding and adhering to standard protocols is crucial for successful collaboration. This shared knowledge facilitates smooth interaction and efficient task execution. This tutorial aims to provide an overview of developing autonomous robots that communicate about tasks and strategies by sharing conventions, emphasizing the importance of high levels of interaction and adaptability to human behaviors.

For mobile robots to navigate unfamiliar environments independently without requiring detailed maps, they need an adaptive system capable of adjusting to new spatial information. This paper suggests an innovative hierarchical topological map representation system, called HiTMap, built on a dual graph structure consisting of a broad, high-level map overviewing the entire environment, and a detailed, low-level map providing precise navigation data. The high-level map dynamically adjusts its intricacy to accommodate changes in its complexity, whereas the low-level map remains standardized in structure but can be updated with newly discovered data. This system allows the robot to decide at each movement stage which map to use, thereby balancing an efficient movement speed with precise local navigation capabilities. Experimental evaluations were conducted using simulated data in fabricated settings and real data collected from a mobile robot operating in a real-world environment.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancement of wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays have been proposed in fields like 3-D imaging, localization, and wireless communications, some of which demand strict adherence to two-dimensional correlation constraints. This paper presents a method for constructing two-dimensional zero-complementary array codes derived from a multivariable function. By leveraging multivariable functions, a novel inter-group complementary code set can be generated that outperforms the traditional set in terms of size. To prove its effectiveness, a multivariable based two-dimensional zero-complementary array code set is proposed. This code set is shown to be achievable by combining multivariable functions with complementary binary sequences and finite fields. By exploiting properties of two-dimensional complementary array codes, it is further demonstrated that the proposed set attains optimal size.

Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used medical imaging technique, but the process of reconstructing images from raw data can be a challenging and time-consuming task, especially when dealing with limited data or mixed noise. To overcome these issues, non-convex total variation has emerged as a promising alternative for reconstructing high-quality images. However, standard variational models struggle to address multiple image reconstruction issues simultaneously, such as removing noise from sensor data and accounting for varying energy-dependent X-ray sources. To address these challenges, researchers have developed new variational models that leverage the unique properties of each issue in an additive and efficient process. These models utilize total variation for noise removal and non-convex data fidelity terms for reconstructing images from multiple energy-dependent X-ray sources. To solve these complex reconstruction problems, researchers have applied advanced numerical methods, such as proximal gradient, gradient projection, and primal-dual algorithms, and have successfully applied these techniques to synthetic and real-world data sets.

We've discovered a fundamental shift in the theory describing light interaction with nanoscale gaps. As these gaps become extremely small, quantum effects override the boundary diffusion approximation, leading to nonlocal responses that vary with material properties. These quantum effects result in an unexpected increase in material absorption, contrasting sharply with traditionally observed decreases. These findings have profound implications for designing future nanodevices, highlighting the need to carefully consider quantum effects for metals like doped semiconducters to minimize absorption, whereas noble metals like gold exhibit increased absorption due to lost quantum effects. Our research sets a new standard for accurately modeling nanoparticle behavior and identifying the precise scale at which devices operate within the nanosecond timescale, where quantum effects become crucial.

In this research, we investigate the impact of term relevance feedback on contextualized named entity retrieval. Specifically, we adapt a classifier-driven combined term-field model to handle re-ranking for contextized entity descriptions, and evaluate its effectiveness using conventional and AI-generated (CLARK) terminology. Our findings indicate significant improvements in conventional descriptives, with average gains of 0.033 and 0.024 for MAP and MRR. Furthermore, we observe comparable performance improvements with CLARK descriptives, averaging 0.029 and 0.024 for MAP and MRR. These results are in line with those of a prior study and highlight the robustness of AI-generated descriptives for contextualized named entity description.

Time stamp-based data, including multivariate time series and longitudinal data, hold a wealth of information, but their complexity often leads to data overload, making interactive exploration essential. The proposed solutions involve designing interactive displays and tools to help analysts discover patterns, anomalies, and inferences. Our approach involves a unified framework for multivariate time-based data and utilizes simple visual displays combined with interactive filtering and selection tools. We validate the need and effectiveness of the designed tools through a study of 12 experts analyzing a hospital's electronic patient record data, focusing on identifying trends in their health conditions.

A widespread method for representing electronic health records (EHRs) involves using a graph neural network (GNN) similarity approach, where each patient is a node in the graph, and an edge signifies similarity between patients. Existing graph-EHR methods primarily use a uniform similarity measure for all patients, creating a heterogeneous-EHR graph for further analysis. To address this limitation, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity GNN (HSGNN) model. This model employs a similarity measure tailored to each patient, taking into account their clinical and demographic attributes when calculating similarity. An innovative method is proposed to compute similarity scores using statistical moments, which can handle varying similarity data and are more robust to outliers. Consequently, the HSGNN model allows for more accurate and diverse patient similarity assessments, especially in scenarios with incomplete similarity information. Extensive testing on three large-scale benchmark datasets confirms the superior performance of the HSGNN model over existing methods in predicting patient similarity and related tasks. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/linhtran11/HSGNN.

Using a mean-field approach and incorporating both non-uniform surface charge distribution and surface polarization, we have derived an analytical solution for the electrostatic potential and concentration profiles within the electric double layer resulting from the interaction of a charged soft surface with an electrolyte solution. Notably, our findings demonstrate that when the surface polarization is taken into account, the potential at the point of zero force decreases, the electric double layer thickness increases, and the surface density of counter-ions decreases, suggesting that accounting for surface polarization in the electric double layer is a crucial consideration in the design of soft materials and devices.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured documents is a highly desirable goal. To achieve this goal, several approaches have been explored, including transformation-based techniques, rule-driven methods, and machine learning models. Despite their success in isolated tasks, these approaches have limitations when applied to diverse requirements extraction tasks. We propose a novel decision tree model that utilizes natural language understanding to extract unstructured requirements from documents. This approach was tested on four datasets spanning four different tasks: sentence classification, entity recognition, boolean rule generation, and rule application for data annotation and classification. The proposed model, when combined with pre-existing data and rules, performed competitively on four benchmark datasets. This study highlights the significance of integrating human knowledge through decision trees with natural language understanding, as well as using domain-specific rules to annotate and classify unstructured data.

This research introduces an energy-efficient protocol in a multi-hop cooperative network, aiming to optimize the duration nodes can operate on a limited battery by extending the system's lifetime. A proposed relay scheduling scheme maximizes network coding opportunities, while another power allocation method minimizes transmission power for scheduled relays. In addition, the researchers propose an alternative approach scheduling all relays and allocating power optimally. Simulation results show that the proposed schemes significantly extend the system's lifetime compared to existing methods.

A theoretical framework combining relativistic effects and quantum mechanics to describe superconducting systems with localized magnetic impurities has been developed. This framework was tested using the example of a manganese atom placed on a niobium surface, and it was discovered that it accurately predicts certain characteristics of the resulting states, albeit with some discrepancies in others. While there was agreement in terms of the relationship between state energy and magnetic field, there were differences in terms of minimum energy positions and phase transitions due to magnetic field. It was suggested that the theoretical framework might be limiting the accuracy due to using an approximate description of the electronic structure, neglecting some magnetic interactions, and using an idealized infinite surface model.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) are commonly used
for map registration in mobile robotics, but they can be sensitive to registration
initialization, resulting in poor performance or failure to register. This paper
introduces an effective approach to address this issue, utilizing distribution-regression
neural networks to create a filter that corrects NDT transform parameters and improves
NDT's performance. We tested this method in both simulated and real-world scenarios,
and it consistently achieved highly accurate results with minimal computational cost,
outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Satellite images are widely utilized across various domains, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and security, among others. However, satellite 
imagery often contains obstacles or inaccuracies, necessitating the application 
of image processing techniques. Although deep networks have gained prominence, 
they have limitations such as a need for significant computational resources and 
the risk of overfitting. In this study, we present two novel edge detection 
algorithms specifically tailored for satellite images, aiming to overcome the 
shortcomings associated with deep networks. By combining mathematical 
operations rather than relying on parameter learning, these algorithms can 
effectively identify edges. Furthermore, we investigate the application of 
these novel edge detection methods to the segmentation of satellite images. 
Through numerical assessments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed 
methods compared to established techniques such as Sobel filters and deep 
learning-based solutions.

To study and compare Non-linear X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectra (XANES) signals generated at a fluence of 10 mJ/cm^2 from a TiO2 sample, we employed three different model types. These models included one based on Full Multiple-Scattering Theory for the initial state formation and two different approaches for the final state: a model using a Gaussian distribution for the final state and a second model using a rate model to describe the electron population dynamics.

The application of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) in automatically categorizing modulations has shown to be effective. However, its performance can deteriorate significantly when faced with adversarial inputs, leading to the consideration of a more resilient classification system. This research presents a pioneering study in developing a resilient modulation classification model that can withstand adversarial attacks. The proposed model combines a discriminator within a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with a probability distribution generated by the discriminator to match the natural input modulation distribution. The GAN-discriminator system enhances the discriminator's robustness against adversarial inputs, making it more resilient to classification challenges. The results of the study demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model in achieving accurate modulation classification even under adversarial conditions. A comparative analysis of the proposed model is provided against a standard Bayesian Approach (BA) and a standard Deep Learning (DL) approach.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a complex task due to the
homogeneous appearance of the brain, making it a challenging problem for
automated diagnosis. To address this, deep convolutional neural networks have
been used successfully, particularly those that specialize in brain image
analysis. However, these models often face the limitation of generalization
when applied to new domains, a problem known as domain generalization
shortcomings. To tackle this issue, domain adaptation and domain
randomization techniques have been developed, allowing models to be more
effective when trained on data from different hospitals and to
recognize lesion patterns that are common across different datasets
despite variations in imaging and protocol details. This study compares the
performance of domain adaptation, domain randomization, and continuous
learning approaches, evaluating their ability to segment MS lesions
automatically.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measure spaces with contrasting polar mass distributions is demonstrated.
When considering趋向  Euclidean space, we see that this comparison method converges to the traditional bipolar formulation of the Ma-Trudinger-Aubin inequality.
We establish a measure-theoretic analogue of the bipolar Alexandrov comparison principle and employ it to prove a Euclidean analogue of the bipath contraction principle.
We demonstrate that, for manifolds with non-negative Ricci curvature, solutions to the bipolar Monge-Ampere equation yield optimal transport maps that conform to the bipolar contraction of paths principle.

The success of the deep learning community in tasks such as chess and speech recognition has piqued interest in applying deep neural networks (DNNs) to scientific modeling. However complex events with significant uncertainty are often beyond the capabilities of available networks. To address this limitation, a new framework is introduced that enables the use of DNNs to capture the discrepancies between events simulated by a physical model at fine temporal and spatial resolutions. Framework components include a method for training DNNs using limited and noisy data, an approach to assess the trained networks' reliability, and a method to leverage the networks to improve predictions of physical systems. Framework efficacy is demonstrated in experiments with a simplified atmospheric convection model, which also shows that using DNNs to accelerate convection calculations enhances convergence rates of related stochastic methods.

A detailed VLA study of the Dragon IRD core revealed its massive density structure. By using C$^{18}$O, C$^{17}$O, and CS emission, researchers measured the core's mass and derived its thermal structure. The core initially displayed the typical thermal profile, with its central area being the hottest at temperatures of 15-20 K. Notably, its mass was estimated to be around 1400 solar masses within a radius of 0.42 pc, making its central area mass-equivalent approximately 160 solar masses. The critical mass for gravitational collapse was found to be 600 solar masses within a radius of 0.35 pc. Furthermore, its core mass-growth rate was found to exceed that of other star-forming regions, reaching a velocity of 0.35 solar masses per year. To determine the impact primordial black holes have on the formation of cosmic structures, we employed the PopSyCLE Python program to model dark primordial black holes. We employed four primordial black hole mass ranges, starting from 10-10 to 10-16 solar masses, and two initial primordial black hole abundance levels of 0.01 and 0.1, resulting in a total of eight distinct simulations. We compared these simulations to standard Lambda CDM cosmological models, which do not account for primordial black holes. Our initial simulations revealed that primordial black holes in the mass range of 10-19 solar masses significantly affect the formation of cosmic structures, particularly when their abundance is 10 percent or more of the cosmic mass. However, primordial black holes in other mass ranges do not noticeably influence the formation of cosmic structures across all of the scenarios tested. Our study indicates that primordial black holes in the mass range of 10-19 solar masses can be used to constrain their abundance to less than 0.001, particularly when considering Planck mission data and data from the formation of reionization.

We conducted research into systems made up of uniform wedge-shaped particles consisting of spheres. These particles have a conical shape, and their bases are perfectly smooth. By using advanced computer simulations, we were able to investigate the systems' phase behavior. Our research revealed distinct regions of crystalline behavior, including novel crystalline forms such as a trimer gas, liquid, body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed structures. In addition, we found a trimer crystal phase characterized by a honeycomb arrangement, and phases featuring periodic structures of splay modulations in both shape and density for certain wedge shapes. These novel phases indicate the existence of a triple point and suggest the presence of multiple transition lines within this system.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize modifications to the base model, allowing us to incorporate fewer parameters while adapting to our needs. We introduce the Special Token Adaptation (STA) method to achieve this by integrating trainable special tokens into the model. These tokens facilitate a more strong representation learning and better feature alignment for each task. We demonstrate through experiments on five benchmarks that STA outperforms other adaptation techniques. Moreover, we show the effectiveness of combining multiple special tokens for multi-task learning, and analyze the effect of token type and placement on performance.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection by comparing the value of sets after adding specific elements. The existing literature employs a multi-dimensional scaling approach to model the set values, utilizing observed set comparisons to calculate the set values. However, this standard approach may not fully capture how context can influence these comparisons due to limitations in offering comparable alternatives at a time. To address this, the paper introduces a novel experimental design that enables participants to express their preferences among sets within distinct contexts, where they are aware of the set values of other options. This new design allows for the derivation of additional constraints that are not available using the standard approach, highlighting the significance of considering set contexts when making judgments. To illustrate this, the paper presents an experimental study on binary set additions, where the results reveal that the more information participants have about the sets, the more likely they are to notice inconsistencies in their judgments. Furthermore, the data suggests that participants may use set contexts to implicitly consider unobservable factors when making their judgments.

Our approach to analyzing polymer glass-forming liquids relies on the assumption that a transition occurs between equilibrium liquid and glassy states, where the balance shifts from thermodynamic equilibrium to kinetic 'arrest'. This concept, known as the thermodynamic-dynamic interrelation, is investigated in detail through the analysis of configurational entropy, enthalpy, and volume in terms of an extensive variable representing the balance between kinetic and thermodynamic equilibria. By fitting experimental data to this theoretical framework, key quantities such as the activation energy and a coefficient describing the temperature dependence of the glass transition are obtained for various polymers near their glass transition temperature, including polystyrene, polybutadiene, and polyisoprene.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, which often necessitates negation handling. We examine this issue through developmental lens, leveraging existing research on human negation acquisition. We break down negation handling into five categories, rooted in cognitive development, linguistics, and psychology. Analyzing the capabilities of multiple Transformer-based models with varied architectures and training data, we discover that these models do not master all negation handling aspects. Moreover, our findings suggest that pre-training on large corpora can enhance model performance, and that tailored negative examples may be needed to teach models more complex negation handling abilities.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now a standard component,
enabling the network to select source positions relevant to the translation task.
However, the current attention mechanism solely relies on unknown source positions,
ignoring potential future context. This paper proposes a novel look-ahead attention
model, which can condition future attention weights on source positions already
observed during decoding. By applying the proposed model to a range of languages
pair datasets, the experiment demonstrates its effectiveness in significantly
enhancing generation outcomes in the context of neural machine translation.

This note aims to calculate the weight of Kontsevich for nonlinear invariants of a particular nature: the connection two-form graph $G_{\nabla}$ and the curvature two-form graph $R$. When applied to the Poisson tensor bivector $\pi$ defining a symplectic Poisson structure, we can compute its Kontsevich weight and demonstrate a Kontsevich conformal field theory (CFT) identity $[\pi, \pi] = 0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{CTr} G_{\nabla} = 0$. Our method involves a novel graph interpretation of the CT product formula, combining CT identities with the properties of holomorphic block graphs to bypass the need for string field theory.

This research focuses on large-N, d-dimensional O(N) models, such as the d-dimensional sigma model (d≥4), phi^4 theory in even d≥5, and D=3 sigma model. For each model, we establish a specific, non-zero value for the 2-point sphere CFT coefficient, which we then utilize to solve for the 2 and 3 sphere coefficients in thermal CFTs. Our findings are supported by numerical calculations across all models and dimensions. Building upon our result for 2-point coefficients, we extend to higher dimensions using a generalized approach for n-sphere coefficients. Notably, for n≥2, these coefficients in large-N d dimensions are determined by their corresponding 2-sphere coefficients, allowing for the creation of effective central charges for large-n sphere entropies. Consequently, this method enables the assessment of unitarity for large-n sphere SLCFTs, which is contingent upon 2-sphere coefficients. Large-n sphere SLCFTs, encompassing a variety of scenarios, include states in hot QFTs and subregions of holographic CFTs, and we apply our findings to the sphere entanglement entropy of simple holographic states and provides evidence for the entanglement first law for large-N spheres.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms over prior research by Song (2006) and Muckenhauer and Penev (2015), as well as derive new Euler approximations for discretely monitored options with better convergence rates.

The discovery of high-energy gamma rays from clusters of galaxies has significant implications for understanding the cosmic baryon cycle and particle acceleration. A recent investigation analyzed 14 clusters across the universe, spanning a broad range of redshifts, to predict the impact of gas in these clusters on the surrounding intergalactic space. The study found that the gas covers approximately 10% of the universe, implying an even smaller impact on the extragalactic gamma-ray background, approximately 0.1%. This conclusion is supported by additional research indicating that the gas is primarily concentrated at the centers of the clusters. Assuming that the inverse Compton process generates gamma rays, the predicted signal would be significantly weaker than observed, while electron collisions with cosmic microwave background particles could explain current observations. However, if the gas extends beyond the visible boundaries of the clusters, the scenarios would change, potentially allowing the gas to generate significant gamma-ray flux and extend the extragalactic background down to lower energy thresholds.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This process not only produces distinct non-Gaussian patterns observable in the cosmic microwave background and gravitational waves but also in primordial large-scale structures, offering potential clues about the high-energy physics of inflation. Utilizing classical cosmological collider physics, we demonstrate that a massive particle's oscillations during inflation can imprint a unique signature on cosmological observables, unlike any existing evidence from the LHC. Our analysis highlights that these signatures, especially those from massive particles much larger than the Hubble scale, can be accurately modeled with classical methods, with logarithmically enhanced O(1) effects that can be detected with a next-generation CMB experiment like CMB-S4. Furthermore, if these primordial features also produce tensor modes or larger-scale structures, we suggest that we can directly test a variety of high-energy physical theories, including an alternative to standard inflation, necessitating only the production of massive particles with a mass of around $10^{-2}$ MeV.

Despite achieving remarkable success in computer vision, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are notoriously difficult to interpret. Several attempts have been made to visualize their inner workings by showcasing how they transform input images, but these approaches often overlook the fact that DCNNs are trained to convert raw images into high-level class predictions, essentially transforming visual data into semantic concepts. This research proposes a novel method for DCNN visualization that reveals how each layer converts image and semantic components, offering insights into the network's overall functionality. Our analysis focuses on a ResNet-50 model using the ImageNet dataset, demonstrating that ResNet's first layer captures low-level visual patterns, while intermediate and deeper layers focus on higher-level semantic information. Notably, our explanation resists adversarial perturbations, providing a robust understanding of the network's behavior even under adverse conditions.

Developing a comprehensive microscopic understanding of cuprate superconductivity is essential in uncovering their underlying superconducting mechanism. A substantial body of evidence suggests that the primary mechanism driving one and two-dimensional cuprate superconductivity involves the long-range attraction between particles, which counteracts the strong repulsive Coulomb force. Recent studies have shown that spin-fluctuation and a combination of their effects can produce this long-range attraction, but its magnitude is generally insufficient. Our study, in contrast, uncovers a previously overlooked, even more pronounced long-range attraction, which arises from a single-component charge interaction and is facilitated by longitudinal optical phonons. Notably, this effect is particularly significant at low temperatures and can be further intensified by interactions between electrons and electrons, as well as between electrons and phonons. To address the strong correlations present in cuprates, we employ the Hubbard-Lieb-Ward equations, which, to the lowest non-trivial order, reduce to the Schwinger-Keldysh kinetic equation. By employing the Hubbard-Salams variational double random-phase approximation, we are able to solve these complex non-linear equations and demonstrate that the resulting phonon-mediated interaction can effectively overcome the Coulomb repulsion at low temperatures. Our research also provides a straightforward and straightforward approach to numerically evaluate the attractive interaction, which can be used in future studies.

The ongoing influence of the 2019 novel coronavirus pandemic has created numerous causal queries, with researchers seeking to understand its origin and the most effective countermeasures to mitigate its impact. To address these questions, it's essential to learn causal structures from observational data collected over time. We analyzed the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic dataset, using a structural approach, to explore its underlying causal relationships. By leveraging a large-scale Chinese survey dataset, we investigated how various aspects of people's lives, such as economic conditions and social interactions, contribute to the spread of the pandemic. We assumed that an initial infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 among community members triggers the widespread outbreak. Through simulations and empirical experiments, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in recovering causal structures. Our findings revealed that widespread news reports and social gatherings may contribute to the rapid dissemination of the virus. Additionally, we discovered that factors such as social distancing and public health awareness play a crucial role in controlling the spread of the pandemic.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ with a magnetically metastable state, the magnetic structure undergoes the coexistence of metastable and ground state skyrmion and stripe lattices. Neutron scattering experiments, conducted at a temperature of 1.8 K and varying magnetic fields, revealed a significant change in the skyrmion lattice with the field. Specifically, the lattice showed a progressive shrinkage and then suddenly vanished at ~0.5 T, before gradually reappearing at ~0.7 T and then disappearing again at ~0.9 T, ultimately settling into the ground state skyrmion and stripe lattice around 1.1 T. The first and second transitions correspond to the collapse of the metastable skyrmion lattice, while the re-appearance and subsequent disappearance of the lattice at ~0.7 T and ~0.9 T respectively are indicative of the melting and re-appearance of the metastable lattice in a stripe background. Our findings demonstrate the complexity of the magnetic phase diagram in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ with the coexistence of two distinct skyrmion phases, separated by the re-appearance and disappearance of the metastable lattice, providing a unique opportunity to study the topological phase diagram in this material.
High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are examined, particularly their latest developments and research summary, selective overview, and future pathways are presented.

The equilibrium problem has a broad range of applications, encompassing several problems in mathematical analysis, and is withstood by efficient solution methods, many of which are influenced by the concept of fixed points. This paper aims to demonstrate that the EM-type theore on bounded sets in certain spaces can be derived from Banach's contraction principle, and the set of solutions can be approximated by the fixed points of a specific contraction map under specified conditions on domains and operators. Furthermore, the continuity of a specific mapping is explored on a given domain.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to a surge of interest in Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) for their uncertainty estimation capabilities in image inexact hidden information applications. BNNs' ability to accurately locate inexact hidden information and represent channel reliability can be harnessed for creating more robust image inexact hidden information methods. A new method of reversible inexact hidden information using a Bayesian Neural Network is proposed, utilizing the uncertainty estimation capability for dynamic channel weightation. The experimental results confirm the superiority of the proposed technique over the conventional steganography method using binary weights.

The goal of this research is to understand how convective turbulence impacts global dynamos within a mean-field approach, which involves separating large and small scale motions and representing the effect of the latter on the former through mean-scale advection and turbulent correlation fields. By using direct numerical simulations as a basis, we've created a convective turbulence database and applied it to investigate how these turbulent effects influence a global dynamos. We found that the models' predictions diverge significantly based on the treatment of mean advection, even when the same turbulent transport model is used, indicating that the choice of mean advection model has a substantial influence on dynamos. To better match simulations, we propose a revised approach to calculating turbulent transport that takes into account latitudinal variations in eddy sizes and convective intensities. With this approach in place, we were able to obtain global dynamos that align with simulations across various rotation rates and levels of rotation.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. Observations at 87 GHz detected two jets associated with radio emissions, as well as widespread C+ and O fine structure [C I] 63$\mu$m and [O I] 142$\mu$m emissions, respectively. These [C I] and [O I] emissions exhibit westward moving molecular outflows with velocities of 300-500 km s$^{-1}$, in agreement with those observed in the radio jets. A broad range of velocity offsets, spanning 100 km s$^{-1}$, was also found. A surface brightness of the [C I] emission at the base of the outflow is approximately 100 times higher than that of the [O I] emission. A web of subarcsecond-scale filaments in the region, likely the site of the outflow's origin, was also discovered. A web of these filaments is superposed upon the galaxy's bright, central star-forming area. A web of these filaments is also found in data from the ATLASGAL survey. A web of these filaments is also found in data from the ATLASGAL survey.
