A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations describes quasilinear diffusion. A pathologies-free and efficient numerical approach has been proposed to solve quasilinear diffusion. By utilizing an explicit formula for the tensor of random directional fluctuations, numerical instabilities are avoided. A new method was implemented and tested in a range of magnetized plasma scenarios, showing good results and being suitable for complex environments. Furthermore, through a comparison with other approaches, we observed that at low numerical errors, our method exhibits more consistency in terms of entropy.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems using Nordsieck stepsize doubling methods.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of the inequality ${\langle }T^*u, T^*v{\rangle \leq \rho\|u\|\|v\|, \rho\in(0,1\,], for *equibound* solutions belonging to the space $\bigcap_{t\geq 0}(T^*)^t L$. This equivalence holds in the case where the space X is Hilbert. For Banach spaces X, a solution existence criterion is established for $\bigcap_{t\ >0}(T^*)^t L$ with specific $0<p\leq 1$.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software that facilitates interactions between dimuonium particles and ordinary matter. Designed to support the muonium-capture experiment, MuMuPy computes dimuonium properties like spatial distributions and ionization cross-sections. Furthermore, the software is intended to assist in the muonium-capture experiment, incorporating factors like temperature-dependent interaction cross-sections and scattering processes. The software is available online at https://github.com/jeanlouisvialle/mumpy.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of its competitors. The conventional utility-based method for achieving the minimum variance portfolio fails in this context, so we establish an optimal portfolio selection process for complete markets, which can be fully solved with mathematical precision.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the abundance of metals, and dust, as well as the processes driving their interstellar medium dynamics. The article also explores the similar features observed in dwarf galaxies to those found in the Milky Way, examining the similar stages of galaxy evolution and similar dynamic states. The ultimate goal is to develop a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic state of the interstellar medium within dwarf galaxies through comparison with the similar system observed in our galaxy.

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermionic lattice model with local bosons. A particular scenario is analyzed in detail, in which the fermionic quasiparticles become highly unstable under specific conditions related to their coupling and energy at the boundary of the Brillouin zone. This instability encompasses various phases: from biquark to quark and boson states.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3333383} found that the Thompson groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit uniformly exponential divergence, with the growth rates of non-abelian Thompson groups $T$ and $V$ being more than twice those of $F$. This study generalizes their findings to all standard and braided Thompson groups, generalizing $T$ to $\widehat{G}_n^+$ and generalizing $V$ to $\widehat{G}_n$, with the group $G_n$ lying between $F_n$ and $F_n^+$. Furthermore, we observe that the braided Thompson groups have a larger divergence compared to their non-braided counterparts, with braided $F^+_{n}$ having a more significant divergence rate than $F^+_n$.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the advantages of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been released on the HuggingFace Transformers library.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. A. Aptekarev regarding the orthogonal polynomials.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to obtain high-quality human annotations, such as summaries, poses a significant annotation challenge, specifically in identifying qualified workers who consistently deliver reliable results, as most workers often produce subpar outputs due to the difficulty of distinguishing quality submissions amidst numerous low-quality ones. In this research, we first, through manual inspection, identify the most skilled workers in MTurk for creating word-level summaries, and second, develop an automated evaluation framework to detect these workers. Our findings suggest that developing accurate automatic summary evaluators remains a significant challenge in distinguishing the best workers.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task in natural language processing and computer vision, demands precise temporal understanding of video clips and the ability to retrieve corresponding textual descriptions from an extensive dataset. Recent studies have shown the benefits of hybrid models combining the capabilities of Transformers and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), however, their reliance on handcrafted designs and fixed structures often limits their performance. This paper proposes TS2-Net, a Transformer-based approach designed to capture key temporal information without the constraints of predefined structures. By incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, TS2-Net effectively models text and video sequences at different granularities, resulting in adaptable representations without reliance on traditional CNNs. Experimental findings on three major benchmarks confirm TS2-Net's superiority over its recent state-of-the-art RNN, CNN, and Transformer baselines, as well as hybrid models, achieving impressive results with 100-frame video inputs on multiple benchmarks with significant margin improvements.

We've examined neutral flavor changing currents involving top quarks within the context of the $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R \times U(1)$ gauge theory, where the right-handed quarks exhibit anomalous parity. By incorporating the concept of spontaneous, multi-stage symmetry breaking along with Higgs fields, we've shown that there exists a novel, neutral flavor changing current that connects the $t$- and $c$-quarks. To address the longstanding problem of the $B \to (e\pm)(e\mp)$ decay constraint, we have incorporated an additional symmetry, $U(1)_{X}$, into the $E_6$ model and adjusted the right-handed quark couplings accordingly, effectively eliminating the unwanted $t$- and $c$-quark interaction coupling while preserving the desired $c$-quark coupling on the left side.

In response to the shortcomings of network models based solely with preferential attachment, research has developed directed hybrid networks that combine uniform and preferential attachment mechanisms. These directed networks, formed from an initial seed node, only incorporate new nodes through a random mechanism or existing nodes, respectively. With preferential attachment given a probability and remaining probability distributed among nodes proportionally to their in-degree. These networks, particularly in the limit, follow a power-law distribution in node connectivity. In addition, an exact formula has been found for the probability distribution of node connectivity in these networks, and it was shown that network evolution slows down as the weight given to the initial node increases. This model was further applied to generate synthetic data frames mimicking real-world phenomena and was found useful for one-frame synthetic generation.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems to prevent disruption to licensed services. The initial step in developing such systems is accurately identifying wireless radio transmitters causing interference. This work presents a novel multi-label classification approach to resolve the interference detection challenge faced by a hypothetical terrestrial internet infrastructure listening to the 2.4 GHz ISM band. The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural network to process, analyze, and interpret radio signals, enabling the automatic identification of interfering sources. The approach's effectiveness was demonstrated through rigorous testing on simulated and real-world datasets comprising diverse signal patterns. Comparative assessments against benchmark methods showed superior performance and yielded a proposed architecture achieving a 97.11% mean accuracy in interfering source identification.

To grasp the implications of quantum mechanics within complex cosmic environments, including those featuring gravitation and electromagnetic forces, we have rectified the known inconsistencies in spin-0 and spin-1 Klein-Gordon equations. Focusing on Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic strings that incorporate both dislocation and electromagnetic fields, our investigation into the respective equations reveals efficient correlations between energy and charge, as well as vorticity quantities, contributing to understanding the intricate interplay between quantum mechanics and cosmic phenomena.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions, which are fundamental to particle physics, are crucial in understanding the structure of nucleons. To access these distributions, physicists use deep inelastic electron scattering, specifically with linear accelerators. A notable process, called differential virtual Compton scattering (DVCS), allows researchers to extract certain parton distribution functions called generalized parton distributions (GPDs) and a parton correlation known as the generalised polarized parton distribution function (GPDF). A new observable, $A_U^\perp$, has been identified which provides information about GPD $H^\perp$. This is significant because it's the first observable that can distinguish GPD $H^\perp$ from its counterpart, $\tilde{H}$. To study this observable, researchers need to measure not only electron and photon polarization but also the polarization of the scattered proton. Recent experiments, specifically at the HERMES and JLab facilities, have shown that $A_U^\perp$ is non-zero, with HERMES finding that GPD $H^\perp$ is odd-parity and the same sign as GPD $H$. This work proposes a new experimental setup to measure $A_U^\perp$, involving the polarization of the recoil proton, to distinguish GPD $H^\perp$ from $\tilde{H}$. This would be the first experiment to do so, using data from an accelerator at JLab. To study $A_U^\perp$, the polarization

Artificial intelligence has expanded human capabilities in processing complex information and executing precise tasks through enhanced cognitive and automated systems. Historically, enhancements to human capabilities have been achieved through tool improvements rather than being classified as such. The future of human capabilities will likely be significantly impacted by the integration of advanced AI systems. A crucial question remains: how will future AI systems that surpass human intelligence contribute to the enhancement of human capabilities? To address this, it is necessary to establish a conceptual framework that defines and categorizes the various forms of AI-based enhancements. This paper introduces a framework for understanding the potential AI-based enhancements to human capabilities.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in the presence of strong spin-orbit coupling on a square lattice. The strong spin-orbit coupling leads to the formation of modulated superfluid phases characterized by specific wave patterns. To study the phase transitions within this system, we utilize a finite temperature variational method based on a ten-component Ginzburg-Landau-type free energy framework. The variational method effectively captures the nature of order parameters associated with different phases. Our results show that as interaction strength increases, the system undergoes a phase transition from modulated superfluid to a strongly correlated Minkowski crystal state at a particular interaction parameter. The simulated critical interaction parameter aligns with previous studies at low temperatures. Furthermore, by introducing quantum fluctuations, we find quantum melting occurs within the region of modulated superfluid phases. The temperature dependence of variational temperatures for these phases is explored, revealing their relationship with interaction parameters, lattice depth, and temperature. By adjusting lattice depth, we can manipulate the phase boundaries within the modulated superfluid phase, and our investigation demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in studying thermal properties of this system.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and a group isogeny φ from G_1 to G_2. It follows that for any pair of graphs H_1 that can be represented by G_1 and a surjective local edge labeling φ': V(H_1) → V(H_2) preserving incidence, there exists an isogeny φ such that φ': V(H_1) → V(H_2) corresponds to φ. Notably, we've discovered numerical instances to illustrate the limitations of applying this correspondence to determine the automorphism group of a graph that can be represented by a group G, particularly for the dyadic case where the group order is 2^m, with a record low value of m=6.

Recently, two new solutions in massive Type IIA with $AdS_4$ and nilmanifolds were found by superpotentials. It was discovered that they correspond to the dual of a conformal field theory with chiral algebras, as predicted in a previous work. This paper expands upon these initial findings by also applying this approach to obtain solutions with $AdS_4$ and torus backgrounds. Furthermore, we identify two new solutions in this category through traditional methods. The paper also explores a pair of solutions in massive Type IIA with $AdS_3$ and tori, as well as their interpretations in terms of the 2D coset CFT. Finally, we verify the results of a recent paper on the cohomological determination of 2D CFT duals in a context of cohomology exact triangles obtained from the cohomological supersymmetry charges.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a critical step. Gaussian Process kernel functions, a versatile machine learning tool, allow us to represent complex functions effectively. Nevertheless, finding the right kernel function for a particular task can be quite challenging, especially when dealing with novel data. Our research introduces a method that utilizes Gaussian Arithmetic Expression Trees to represent kernel functions and evolves them to enhance their performance automatically. By treating kernel functions as mathematical expressions, our approach facilitates automatic design and can be easily incorporated into a kernel learning framework. The experiments conducted reveal that Gaussian Arithmetic Expression Trees form valid kernel functions in almost all cases and that our method successfully evolves them to enhance performance, outperforming previous methods when combined with existing Gaussian Process techniques.

Future high-energy muon colliders face a challenge due to in-flight decays of
muons from the beam line, resulting in beam-induced backgrounds (BIB). This
background interference poses a significant obstacle to precise measurements at
such a collider. To overcome this problem, various prevention and mitigation
techniques can be applied, including design modifications of the beam line and
the use of advanced shielding methods. This presentation focuses on experimental
strategies aimed at minimizing BIB, including decisions on detector design,
placement and construction.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. This method effectively transforms sparsity into an optimal transportation problem with an added constraint of differentiability, making it amenable to gradient-based optimization techniques. By leveraging the differentiable nature of Spartan, we explore its impact on generalization through extended training with fixed network size and dynamic network size. Our extended experiments demonstrate that Spartan promotes smaller model sizes, improved generalization on various tasks and architectures, and can even enhance model performance initially by introducing regularized transportation prior.

Theoretical work reveals that in certain conditions under which Bose-Einstein condensation occurs, the Pauli blocking phenomenon emerges as a way to stabilize the system, preventing the unstable growth of certain collective excitations that otherwise cause its decay. This phenomenon is particularly notable when the Pauli blocking condition is bypassed. In the absence of damping, the chemical potential exhibits an effective, temperature-dependent, and negative value - the magnitude of which depends on the temperature and scattering length - causing the system to behave as if it were a highly interacting Bose gas.

Software developers' understanding of how much different types of code defects contribute to its susceptibility to bugs has been studied extensively. Similar to how software engineers can become stuck in unproductive habits due to test code flaws, researchers have investigated whether developers perceive test smell issues as having an impact on severity. Past studies revealed that engineers struggle to accurately assess their severity. Prior knowledge among software engineers, however, has been limited, particularly regarding emerging technologies like Agile and Agile-based testing, where researchers have yet to gather sufficient data. To address this knowledge gap, our study examined the relationship between test smell characteristics and their potential impact on software reliability among Agile-based development teams, and the results showed that test code flaws in design and coupling have significant consequences, while those in behavior and functionality have a lesser effect.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, initially proposed by J.J. Moreau, which involves a differentiable moving set with a speed that can change abruptly. To address this issue, the moving set is replaced with one whose movement speed depends on an integral rather than time itself. This new model, known as an integro-differential sweeping process, has significant real-world applications, particularly in control theory, where it can be used to describe systems with moving constraints, such as vehicles, robots, and cranes. To establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to these problems, we apply sophisticated mathematical tools, including Carathéodory functions, Lipschitz continuous functions, and Ljapunov's inequality. These concepts enable us to prove key results, including the existence and uniqueness of solutions to these problems, as well as their continuous dependence on the initial conditions.

We present the latest version of the KKMCee event generator, specifically designed for precise calculations of electron-positron collisions. Version 6.06, with support for Zγ and Zh production, allows users to model numerous final states including those involving a Z boson, up to four fermions, and multiple photons. By incorporating multiple soft and hard photons, as well as tools for slicing and dipole regularization, the generator is well-suited for use with experimental data. It also includes features for non-radiative processes and offers an estimated runtime, making it efficient to execute on parallel computing systems.

Detecting inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is a critical task in diagnosing and monitoring cardiac conditions, and machine learning models are increasingly being used to automate this process. In this study, the Tiramisu deep neural network is applied to derive inter-beat intervals from rhythmic R-peaks detected in PPG signals, following the preprocessing steps of peak detection, peak-picking, and dynamic time warping. The results show that the network produces accurate predictions, and the study's approach demonstrates accuracy in predicting peaks, inter-beat intervals, and physiological variability, with significantly lower mean squared error compared to peak-to-peak distance methods. Furthermore, the network's ability to reduce mean squared error by over 10 times outperforms conventional methods in peak interval prediction.

To utilize contemporary computing resources efficiently, an randomized algorithm for multiple-pass tensor singular value decomposition (tSVD) has been designed. The algorithm supports any number of parallel processing cores, including GPUs, by introducing a novel memory layout. The layout enables the randomization process to occur in the same memory space as the output, eliminating the need for memory copying. The algorithm produces the same results as the standard two-pass method but is optimized for high-throughput and parallel computing. The algorithm has been integrated into the Armadillo C++ library and is available on the public code repository for further use and integration.

Network analytics heavily relies on embedding static graphs in low-dimensional vector spaces to enable node classification, link prediction, and visualization. Nonetheless, conventional methods primarily focus on static graphs of stable structures and meanings, whereas real-world networks constantly change in both their structural and semantic aspects, necessitating dynamic graph embeddings. To bridge this gap, various approaches have been developed to address the challenge of representing dynamic graphs accurately. This paper surveys the landscape of methods for embedding dynamic graphs, highlighting existing gaps and future prospects to advance dynamic graph representation learning.

Our investigation into the $^7$H ground state uses the Valence Space Valence Valence Cluster Unitary Eddy Model (V$^3$VECM), which is a high-performance computational nuclear physics model capable of handling large-nucleus reactions with many nucleons. By treating $^7$H as a resonance with $^3$H and four nucleons, the V$^3$VECM allows us to calculate its mass, aligning with the mass obtained through the assumption of an unbound five-nucleon system. The calculated $^7$H mass is $6023.823$ MeV/$c^2$, which agrees with the mass found in the experiment by Trka et al., which assumed a $^6$H + n configuration. Our research also demonstrates that the observed width of the $^7$H resonance, measured as $11.62\pm1.23$ MeV, is consistent with its rapid decay.

This research investigates a Dirichlet problem with no data on the boundary in relation to the Nirenberg problem, but on a half sphere. Similar to the Nirenberg problem on the entire sphere, it is an eigenvalue-type problem with a first eigenvalue. By applying the method of non-simple eigenfunctions, we can demonstrate the existence of solutions to this problem, while also deriving geometric conditions for the existence of these solutions.

Deep learning models have become prevalent in research using manifold learning techniques, as they facilitate faster convergence and easier optimization with multiple clusters of high-dimensional data points. Traditional manifold learning methods often produce a basic embedding that may not be suitable for downstream tasks. To overcome this, our work presents Deep SHD, a novel approach that generates a detailed embedding space for representing datasets with multiple groups, resulting in an informative and interpretable space. We demonstrate through experiments that our method is robust and yields superior performance on both unsupervised clustering and supervised classification tasks.

In numerous countries, local health agencies are collaborating with national organizations to conduct contact tracing for COVID-19, a strategy that aims to supplement but not fully replace the efforts of the national system. However, little research has examined how these partnerships affect the effectiveness of contact tracing in containing the virus. Our investigation examined whether and to what extent areas with and without such partnerships experienced variations in their capacity to contain the virus. Using mathematical models, we assessed these effects while accounting for factors such as regional differences in testing capabilities and adherence to contact tracing protocols. Although our findings suggested that the presence of local tracing partnerships was associated with lower R-effective values, a notable factor contributing to better containment in these areas was their tendency to test for a higher proportion of positive cases. Consequently, our conclusions indicated that local tracing partnerships could potentially improve contact tracing outcomes, a benefit that could be further optimized by integrating efficient mass testing strategies.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey, our analysis yields precise distances, masses, and ages for the Melotte 72 open cluster, obtained via multiple analytical methods. By constructing blue horizontal streaks and utilizing blue-R and blue-I photometric data, our study produces a mass estimate of approximately 0.24 solar masses and an age of about 1.6 billion years. These results align with age and mass measurements obtained from other studies, reinforcing our understanding of the open cluster Melotte 72. Our analysis in particular yielded the mass of individual stars within the cluster, yielding an average mass of about 0.24 solar masses with a margin of error of 0.02 solar masses. Age determination yielded a value of about 1.6 billion years with a margin of error of about 200 million years. Our findings for the age, mass, and metallicity of Melotte 72 are consistent with prior studies utilizing different analytical methods.

Data analysis relies heavily on topological tools, which have the advantage of being invariant to data transformations. Traditional methods for computing topological tools become impractical with large datasets, but a different approach, based on combinatorial algebra, allows for efficient calculation when dataset dimensions are slightly larger than the sample size. In the event of general data entries, reducing the data entries to zero inherently changes the data's underlying structure, which motivates the examination of how the changes occur in the case of data entries following a Gaussian distribution, specifically when the number of data points is significantly larger than the sample size, which we call the sparse regime. In the sparse regime, we have made notable advancements by identifying the distribution of a key statistical measure, which helps to control the complexity of the topological tools in the small sample size limit.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using only image features has long been a significant challenge. Previous studies have explored using depth markers or segmentation masks to achieve this, but these approaches are often impractical in real-world scenarios. We introduce a new method for eye-in-Hand self-calibration that relies solely on visual information. We have developed a new neural network architecture, which, along with a data augmentation technique, enables learning the camera's parameters without needing precise 3D scene information. We've also designed a loss function that accounts for scale and rotation ambiguities. Our proposed approach, which is straightforward to implement, outperforms existing methods in both controlled and unsupervised real-world environments, as verified by both numerical simulations and experimental results.

In reinforcement learning applications, prioritizing equity and inclusivity, we address a problem where an inverse controller must be developed to achieve rewards aligned with a desired level of bias. Our approach formulates the bias-constrained reinforcement learning problem as a dual task for the inverse controller, which must produce actions not only biased towards the target outcome but also balanced in other areas. We develop a data-efficient algorithm that learns policies capable of adapting to optimal bias goals while maintaining high rewards. Additionally, we provide theoretical justification for our approach and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulation-based evaluations.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, with the ultimate goal of producing a map to an unparalleled degree of accuracy. This article will examine the mission itself, along with the resulting data releases and their potential impact. A detailed overview of the DR1 and DR2 data releases and their initial findings, including DR1 as a precursor to the eagerly anticipated DR2, will be presented.

For graphs with a given number of vertices, the best achievable vertex separator size for a graph with treewidth $t$ is $\mathcal{O}(t\sqrt{|\mathcal{G}|})$.
This paper presents a new algorithm that computes an $\mathcal{O}(t^2)$-size separator, requiring $|\mathcal{G}|^{2/3}$ words of RAM.
The study addresses this problem in multiple contexts: 
a) By adapting a previously known result, it's possible to find a separator of size $\mathcal{O}(t\sqrt{|\mathcal{G}|})$ using $|\mathcal{G}|^{2/3+\varepsilon}$ words.
b) Another open problem is the existence of an $|\mathcal{G}|^{1/2+\varepsilon}$-size separator, which can be solved affirmatively, requiring $|\mathcal{G}|^{1/3+\varepsilon}$ words.
c) The study also explores whether an $|\mathcal{G}|^{1/3+\varepsilon}$-size separator can be found, which it affirms, requiring $|\mathcal{G}|^{2/3+\varepsilon}$ words.
The last two results resolve long-standing open problems from computational geometry and graph theory, specifically for planar graphs where the known upper bound is $\mathcal{O}(|\math

A significant challenge in network analysis is the development of meaningful methods to incorporate edge weights into network data. Weighted networks can be derived from various sources, such as direct observations (e.g., time spent together) or inductive inferences (e.g., a positive emotional connection). We propose a framework for interpreting and evaluating cluster algorithms for directed networks, considering the three main types of cluster concepts: closed, selective, and efficient. We establish criteria for these interpretations and discuss their applicability to both directly measured and inferred network characteristics. We introduce the application of the Nonnegative Matrix Factorization technique to determine cluster qualities based on a set of weights. We analyze how a unit of weight affects the outcomes, considering equal or non-equal scaling, as well as the impact of direction and noise on the results. We conclude by suggesting that effective and efficient clustering is the most relevant interpretation for certain types of induced weights.

In the context of solving partial differential equations with physics-informed neural networks, the absence of established evaluation criteria for solution accuracy has been addressed. We introduce a concept of certified PDE solutions and develop a corresponding error estimation method for physics-informed neural networks. This approach relies on the training data's distribution, the neural network's architecture, and its learned parameters. Our results offer theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of these solutions without requiring prior knowledge of the problem, thus providing an unreliable-supervisor-free, a posteriori error estimation and adaptive training framework. Furthermore, the developed framework's efficacy is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments involving linear and non-linear problems.

For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in big data analytics and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks. This discussion highlights recent breakthroughs and proposes standard procedures for developing more precise air pollution models grounded in geostatistics and machine learning principles.

Our novel approach centers on separating the Majorana peak from other potential peaks within tunneling spectra produced by Majorana edge modes at the ends of topological nanowires. To accomplish this, we suggest performing tunneling spectroscopy on the Majorana edge mode using a resistor as the tunneling electrode, whose resistance matches the fundamental charge dispersal rate in topological superconductivity, producing a distinct Pauli exclusion effect that clearly distinguishes the Majorana edge mode from other possible edge modes such as Andreev bound states or Bogoliubov states. Furthermore, the major outcome emphasizes that topological superconductivity at the edge of Majorana requires quantum coherence.

We establish a novel approach for exploring action selection in linear contextual bandits, addressing the limitations of existing algorithms, including high computational and memory requirements, by developing a fully policy-agnostic technique. This approach is particularly beneficial for linear bandits with extensive action spaces, where it yields substantial improvements in time and space complexity, thus enabling the efficient model training and deployment of sophisticated bandits with large action spaces on resource-constrained devices. Furthermore, this methodology has significant implications for real-world offline exploration applications.

Graphene with a gap and specific properties can exhibit the orbital Hall effect in certain conditions. Our study demonstrates that under these conditions, the orbital Hall effect can be observed even without a specific magnetic field. When the Haldane model is applied to gapped graphene, current carriers experience this effect due to their specific orbital behavior. The overlap in graphene bands can lead to a valley Hall effect, but in monolayer graphene, the orbital Hall effect becomes the dominant phenomenon. To study this effect experimentally, we propose using a novel setup involving a substrate and a back-gate, allowing for the adjustment of the energy gap in the graphene and the appearance of a transverse voltage in the system.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models, which can be exploited by intentional attacks from data providers. A notable example is the poisoning of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), which aggregate neighboring node features to form representation spaces for further processing in graph-based tasks. Existing research has primarily focused on single-classification tasks, neglecting the complexity of multi-class settings. To address this gap, we propose a new framework for GCN poisoning attacks that considers both target label prediction accuracy and the required samples for classification, which was unexplored in previous work. Our method outperforms baseline attacks on a specific metric while needing significantly fewer samples to achieve the same results, offering a more efficient solution to attacks.

The process of matching objects across different catalogs is a fundamental aspect of astronomical research, which is typically approached using photometric and astrometric attributes. Recent advancements involve employing machine learning algorithms to enhance the matching process based solely on astrometric data, which typically relies on mean coordinates and angular distances between objects. However, we demonstrate that incorporating astrometric quadrupole moments and object magnitudes results in highly effective performance. Furthermore, we find that training data comprising images and corresponding astrometric data from available source lists significantly outperforms traditional approaches relying on randomly distributed data, yielding comparable results to image-only training sets for the matching task.

Infinite hypergraphs whose edges consist of more than two vertices and whose minimal vertex covers have been examined in this paper. We demonstrate that if the hypergraph's vertex set can be mapped one-to-one to a specific type of ordered cardinal $\kappa^+$, then the existence of a $<\kappa$-closed ultrafilter implies a particular type of minimal vertex cover of size $\kappa$. Additionally, the paper delves into exploring the existence of minimal vertex covers in infinite bipartite hypergraphs with degree $\kappa$, starting with $[2,\kappa)$-covered cases. We define a specific type of bipartite hypergraph, known as ABH, and examine its existence under certain conditions, such as the existence of a $\kappa$-complete ultrafilter.

Ontologies that use graphs to represent data can become difficult to comprehend when they contain complex associations. To address this, OntoPlot, a visualisation tool, has been developed to depict a subset of Graph Ontology languages, including OWL2QL, by representing them on directed weighted plots. Compared to traditional directed graphs, OntoPlot has several benefits, including a higher descriptive capacity, easier detection of potential circular associations, and greater scalability for larger datasets. OntoPlot has been extensively tested with real-world data, including a medical and biological ontology, and was found to effectively showcase a wide range of associations between entities that were previously obscured in traditional graphical representations.

We introduce an innovative technique that utilizes CycleGAN for semi-supervised Automatic Speech Recognition with cross-domain language models as an additional constraint. The proposed framework consists of two main components: a cycle-adversarial training framework that ensures the speech distribution remains consistent when transferred between domains, and an inter-domain loss that maximizes shared representations across labeled and unlabeled datasets. Our experiments demonstrate the feasibility of cross-domain Adaptation and show that these cycle-adversarial frameworks effectively improve the performance of speech-to-text models when applied to various datasets.

A fundamental theory called Active Inference explains how agents interact with their surroundings, making decisions that minimize prediction errors by adapting to both the world and themselves. In the context of a robot navigating through familiar spaces, our model leverages a deep neural network to simulate Active Inference, enabling decision-making through predictions of sensory inputs, rather than traditional reward-based learning. Two experiments were conducted to assess the model's performance, demonstrating its ability to efficiently learn navigation from fixed rewards and rapidly adapt to changing environments without requiring retraining.

We have developed a theory to understand the Soret effect in mixtures of small molecules and soft molecules with flexible configurations. Our analysis reveals that Soret coefficients of such mixtures are influenced by two Soret coefficients of mixtures consisting solely of small molecules. The first Soret coefficient, which correlates with the average size of small molecules, always produces a thermal pressure gradient directed towards the cold region. The second Soret coefficient, which relates to the molecular shape asymmetry of the soft molecules, can generate a thermal pressure gradient in either direction. By considering both spherically symmetric spheroids and molecules with multiple degrees of freedom, we confirm the validity of this theoretical prediction.

Automated writing assessment systems play a crucial role in both educational settings and professional recruitment, typically being carried out by specialized platforms. Traditional character-based language models struggle to effectively process natural language in these applications, whereas more advanced transformer-based systems often fail due to excessive computational requirements. We present a novel approach using efficient transformer-based models like ERNIE-M and RoBERTa, enhanced by the inclusion of domain-specific features from expert raters, for the development of an automated essay assessment system. In our experiments using 8555 essays from the CHES_eval 2021 dataset, an approach based on ERNIE-M achieved top quality and accuracy results, with an average correlation of 0.742 with human ratings in a single model test and 0.73 in a split test environment, surpassing the evaluation benchmarks set by the CHES competition for both metrics. Notably, our approach required less than a minute to process each new essay for assessment.

One of the most significant issues in Pedestrian Affinity Search (PAS) based domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the problem of unverified target box re-ranking. Domain shift causes the top predicted boxes from PAS to differ significantly from ground truth, resulting in false positives and a suboptimal trade-off between precision and recall. In response, researchers have proposed various top box re-ranking methods to address this issue. In particular, unsupervised top box re-ranking has gained attention. In this work, researchers propose an unsupervised top box re-sampling method, which, in contrast to existing methods, generates diverse, high-quality negative samples. These samples enable a more effective distribution learning approach without the need for a separate model or handcrafted features. In comparison to existing methods, our proposed approach achieves a substantial improvement in mean average precision (mAP) on ADE20K and PASCAL-PADE datasets.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices to mitigate issues such as noise and distortion. The proposed approach combines two advanced deep learning techniques, incorporating novel modules to improve audio translation and reproduction. Firstly, it utilizes a modified time-frequency masking technique paired with OC-Vocoding to reduce noise while preserving color and texture in high-quality audio. Secondly, it employs a specific module to adjust the properties of noisy audio before it is fed into OC-Vocoding, resulting in improved audio translation and reduced vocoder-induced distortions. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Our primary objective is to gain a deeper understanding of the throwing motion by virtual agents. To achieve this, we examined the impact of point of release errors on the complexity of throwing gestures. Our results indicate that virtual agents respond by modifying motion elements other than the thrower's intended target, such as limb trajectories and timing. Furthermore, we observed the virtual recipient's response in terms of adjusting their posture and moving their head to avoid the thrown object.

To enhance performance in Neural Machine Translation with output-driven decoding, we propose a tree structured decoding approach that incorporates syntax-based connections. Our proposed syntax-guided attention mechanism enables structured, hierarchical sampling of words and phrases. For the direct connection between syntax nodes, we suggest a tree structured decoding method that enables multiple possible paths between them. Experimental results show that adding syntactic connections and enabling structured sampling of phrases significantly improve NMT performance.

The interpretation of observational data in astrochemistry relies on a comprehensive understanding of interstellar molecular surface chemistry, which heavily relies on the binding energy of species adsorbed on dust grain surfaces. However, experimental data of such binding energies are scarce, and existing astrochemical models often lack these values, resorting to the widely-used Raimes-Rappert equation to estimate the bonding strength. In response to this need, a new computational platform has been developed to generate binding energy distributions for covalent and hydrogen bonds between a broad range of species and grain surface sites, utilizing quantum chemical calculations in periodic environments with appropriate point charges to mimic the surface charges.

A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model for the lower bounds is developed based on the underlying data. The model's parameters are statistically determined using a maximum likelihood approach and a likelihood function is created for the multiplicative process, incorporating the lower bounds as inputs. The probability density and cumulative distribution functions for the new model are also provided. The novelty of this work lies in the incorporation of the lower bounds into the probabilistic model, where their influence on the data distribution is explicitly acknowledged. The novel model's potential for accurate time series analysis and forecasting is supported by simulation results and successful applications to data from three real-world systems.

We offer novel approaches to acquiring in-depth knowledge about complex quantum systems using shallow Clifford measurements. Specifically, we present modified algorithms derived from shadow tomography and Liouvignment that utilize lower-depth circuits with minimal performance loss, including similar sample requirements and time efficiency. In addition, we present "cascaded shadows" for estimating statistical expectations across multiple system slices using low-depth circuits with controlled long-range interactions, including shallow shadows, where circuit depth increases only logarithmically with the number of slices, and can be applied even when there is no spatial structure among the slices. Furthermore, our approach allows for a controllable trade-off between circuit depth and sampling efficiency. Our findings demonstrate the value of low-depth circuits in estimating crucial system properties experimentally, and we anticipate Shallow shadows will be particularly useful for studying disordered systems and quench dynamics.

The researchers in a particular study derived an explicit formula for the reflection coefficient $R(k)$ associated with the scattering problem from the Davey-Stewartson II equations in 2D. They solved this scattering problem for a specific type of initial condition with exponentially decaying amplitudes as the spatial coordinate approaches infinity in both positive and negative directions. Building upon the findings of a previous study, they used contour deformation techniques and the residue theorem to develop asymptotic estimates for the reflection coefficient $R(k)$ as the wavenumber $k$ approaches infinity. Notably, for a generic initial condition, $R(k)$ behaves like $\mathcal{O}(|k|^{-1})$, whereas in scenarios where specific residue terms vanish, $R(k)$ behaves like $\mathcal{O}(|k|^{-2})$. This work generalizes a specific case treated by a different study and, similarly, confirms the validity of the corresponding results for the Davey-Stewartson I equations presented in a different study.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) text data is often categorized in a supervised way. In NLP, data augmentation has become a key technique for improving robustness to adversarial attacks and enhancing performance when labeled data is limited. To address these issues, we propose CSE, a novel approach that performs synchronized transformations using multiple input types, and proposes two types of input: a semantic one based on word embeddings, and a syntactic one based on part-of-speech tags. CSE incorporates input pruning, a strategy for adapting to varying data distributions in data imbalanced learning, and is shown to outperform existing methods such as dropout and augmentation techniques in improving classification accuracy and enhancing data imbalance resistance and adversarial robustness on the AG News and IMDB datasets. Our results demonstrate that CSE achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly outperforms recent data augmentation methods, and matches the performance of dropout-based baselines.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experiences to efficiently learn new tasks by representing them in a higher-dimensional space. In this work, we propose a framework inspired by neural networks that enables the representation of previously encountered tasks through linear transformations, and we provide a theoretical basis for this approach based on the convexity assumptions of the underlying functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method when the underlying functions are actually non-convex. A general procedure for developing meta-learning algorithms is presented, and specific algorithms are illustrated through examples involving gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent methods.

Achieving high performance multilingual machine translation with limited or no parallel data is a significant challenge.  Existing solutions, such as data distillation and model quantization, can help overcome this hurdle.  In this study, we compare the effectiveness of post-training model quantization and data distillation in achieving high-performance MT models.  Additionally, we investigate the effect of combining post-training quantization with data distillation to further improve translation performance in resource-constrained settings.  Our findings indicate that while data distillation benefits from this approach, post-training quantization does not.  Consequently, we find that the combination of post-training quantization and data distillation does not yield significant improvements over data distillation alone, leading us to suggest data distillation as a more reliable and stable method for MT in low-resource scenarios.
We introduce a hypergraph with a Lagrangian density that is irrational, along with alternative illustrations featuring irrational Lagrangian densities originating from number theory.

The accuracy of chest X-ray diagnosis for chest diseases, particularly pneumonia, can be significantly enhanced through the use of machine learning-based segmentation techniques, which rely on extensive labelled data. However, acquiring such data can be costly and time-consuming, driving interest in methods that can reduce the amount of labelled data needed. This paper explores this issue further by investigating how different image manipulation techniques can be applied to reduce the amount of labelled data required for accurate segmentation of opacities in the lungs. Various image manipulation methods, including data augmentation and image synthesis, are examined to evaluate their effectiveness in this context. Experimental results show that adaptive image augmentation is the most effective method, achieving better outcomes with less labelled data than other approaches. This research contributes to the development of more efficient data-driven approaches for identifying chest diseases from radiological images.

Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions tailored to user input. We aim to develop image captioning systems capable of generating input-driven captions by framing the task as a prompt-based completion problem. To achieve this, we suggest using a flexible encoder that can adapt to various prompts and a configurable decoder. We further refine our approach by employing advanced prompt engineering techniques, including learning specific token embeddings and using a modifiable memory component. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of this method, showing improvements over current state-of-the-art techniques across multiple captioning-related benchmarks and under different prompt conditions.

A fundamental aspect of any ethical theory is a comprehensive understanding of harm, yet no such definition exists currently. Currently, discussions of harm are predominantly found within the context of utilitarianism, emerging case-by-case and lacking a unifying concept of harm. Moreover, existing philosophical and common perceptions of harm are overly broad and fail to address harm in specific instances effectively. Additionally, their causal nature, if present, remains underexplored and poorly developed. Drawing from the philosophy of science in causal reasoning, I propose an original definition of harm, which characterizes harm as the effect of a cause that differs in outcome from a nearby alternative cause, resulting in a worse outcome.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with popular ecosystems like Jupyter and Bazel is also highlighted. To demonstrate the potential of MMLSpark, the paper presents a significant achievement: a PyTorch model seamlessly combined with an Apache Spark distributed system, enabling seamless scalability and flexibility for complex deep learning tasks.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches to speech-to-text translation leverage separate recognition and translation models, which can benefit from shared multilingual vocabularies derived from audio-to-text and text data. The challenge in training accurate zero-shot translation systems using only shared vocabularies and separate model components lies in the lack of direct target data. To address this issue, we developed a text synthesis system that generates synthetic speech data using acoustic manifold modeling. This synthetic speech data was then utilized to create a dictionary of multilingual words for training zero-shot speech-to-text translation. Acoustic manifold modeling was found to be effective in learning speech data distributions, while our proposed zero-shot speech-to-text translation approach leveraged the proposed method to produce results comparable to state-of-the-art multilingual speech-to-text translation models on news translation tasks. Future research directions to improve the performance of zero-shot speech-to-text translation include refining synthetic speech data and vocabulary generation methods.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations of Coleman-Gurtin type, featuring dynamic boundary conditions in the context of Cox's formulation, as well as Neumann and Robin boundary conditions. Furthermore, we examine a variant of the Coleman-Gurtin equation with memory that relies on the integral of the Laplacian's second order along the object's boundary, rather than the boundary value of the Laplacian, and ultimately addresses a metrical realization issue concerning the distinct diffusive models presented.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions. Our approach leverages the adaptability of deep learning time series models, enabling an ensemble of such models to be combined and yield more accurate results. Additionally, this method effectively handles the challenge of predicting daily energy consumption peak loads, which often proves more difficult than average load forecasts.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating domain expertise with machine learning models stems from the absence of a unified approach to this process. In an effort to bridge this gap, a roadmap has been developed to summarize methods for incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning. The initial step in this process involves categorizing the source of domain knowledge into three distinct groups: (1) knowledge embedded within the model's design; (2) knowledge derived from a domain-specific algorithm; and (3) knowledge applied at the sample level. Within these groups, various operators and techniques have been proposed to incorporate domain knowledge into a model, generally falling into five types: regularization, loss function modification, feature engineering, meta-learning, and knowledge editing.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite advancements in deep learning techniques. The primary issue arises from data imbalance and the inherent biases within datasets, which result in subpar model performance. To tackle this concern, we'll examine the effects of data imbalance and bias on COVID-19 detection models, then introduce an innovative framework, Weakly Supervised Transfer Learning (WS-TL), which effectively balances and diversifies datasets, thus minimizing bias. WSTL uses a Siamese network architecture, leveraging joint supervision from image and patch-level cues. Through our comprehensive study, we demonstrate the efficacy of WS-TL's approach, which shows state-of-the-art results on the public COVID-19 chest CT scan dataset, COVID-Net.

Accurate 3D localization and identification of vertebrae in spinal diseases is a crucial step, but currently, it remains a labor-intensive task. To address this, we propose an integrated framework, combining direct cortical and spinal cord segmentation with more advanced techniques. Our method, leveraging a combination of anatomical principles and scene understanding, employs a space-partitioning strategy guided by anatomical constraints to accurately model vertebrae boundaries and centroids. Our framework is evaluated on two public datasets and demonstrates superior performance to existing methods.

Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a contained environment. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an intertwined electron-photon system confined at the boundary of the cavity. This effect significantly alters the electron's ability to penetrate the barrier and significantly modifies the previously observed suppression of tunneling.

In this research, we approach quadruped locomotion as a control issue rather
than a challenge related to learning, considering the actuator type as the key
factor. An adaptable control framework using compliant actuators, exemplified by the Spring-Actuated Series Elastic Actuator (SASEA), is first introduced.
Next, a deep reinforcement learning approach, based on a state space designed to be independent of scaling, is employed, and also task-state dependent compliance
learning. Consequently, our agent learns a policy that adapts both control and
actuator specifics. Interestingly, our findings demonstrate that deep reinforcement
learning combined with our proposed actuator model and compliance learning method
significantly outperforms traditional spring-actuated Model Predictive Control
(MPC) methods in achieving locomotion, as well as reaching and kicking tasks.

We propose a new variational strategy for calculating the separability norm in **qudit** systems composed of two particles. This method has been put to the test in a numerical study, demonstrating that the proposed strategy achieves the optimal result in certain key scenarios. Furthermore, we show that for certain key scenarios, this method allows for an efficient estimation of the absolute value of the ROSETTA measure, confirming its characteristics as an area of zero curvature.

A well-documented phenomenon in a finite, flat current sheet called the electron-tearing instability occurs at a specific scale, just above electron collisional effects, where it strongly influences magnetic flux structures. This scale remains poorly understood in terms of linear growth rates and the balance between various energies.  Using analytical and numerical methods within a purely electron framework with a finite electron temperature effect, we found that the growth rate of the instability is proportional to the Alfv\'en speed and the electron temperature to magnetic field ratio, validating empirical observations from previous studies and revealing a previously proposed relation's inaccuracy.  Moreover, we observed that the scale of the instability is governed by the balance between magnetic field gradient effects, electron temperature effects, and electron collisional effects, leading to two distinct power laws depending on a specific criterion.  These findings are supported by our results and have implications for understanding similar phenomena in plasmas with finite, flat current sheets and those with strongly sheared flow profiles, particularly in space and astrophysical contexts.

A surge in demand for search techniques has led researchers to explore computer vision-based image retrieval. While traditional methods involve searching a database of images using a query image, a new approach, known as attribute manipulation, enables users to find specific images by modifying attributes in a base image, such as changing the color of clothing or a person's hair color. This method, called fashion image retrieval, is a form of fine-grained attribute manipulation specifically for the fashion industry. Although significant progress has been made in this area, current techniques rely on precise annotations and images at the image-level, which can be costly and difficult to obtain. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new semi-supervised method for fashion image retrieval that operates at the feature-level. This approach generates pseudo-labels for attributes by leveraging the properties of a query image, allowing it to perform fashion image retrieval with minimal supervision. By training a neural network with pseudo-labels generated in this manner, we achieve state-of-the-art results on popular fashion image retrieval benchmarks.

The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ is defined as the solution $x$ to the operator equation $Ax=y$ that minimizes the support function over a convex set, where $\Phi$ denotes the support function and $Y$ is a symmetric convex subset in $X^*$. In the case where $A$ is linear and continuous, this problem can be reformulated as the following dual optimization problem: minimize the functional $f(t)=$$\|\Lambda^*A^*\widehat{p}\|_X^*+$$\|\Lambda^*q\|_X^*$ over the interval $[0,\infty]$, where the functional $f(t)$ is known as the dual gradient flow. This problem can be solved by applying the forward-backward splitting method. Through thorough analysis, it has been proven that the functional $f(t)$ is convex and lower semicontinuous, and therefore has a minimum. By leveraging this property, it can be shown that the corresponding minimizer satisfies the operator equation $Ax=y$ and corresponds to the $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$. Through numerical experiments, the proposed method has been validated for various underdetermined equations with different choices of $X$, $\Lambda$, and $\Omega$.

Constructing the cost function is a key step in estimating light field depth.
The loss of texture information due to occlusion during cost construction can severely compromise the accuracy of depth estimation.
Although occluded regions are recognized in light field tensors, current cost construction methods still rely on matching similar texture features within these regions.
In this paper, a new approach to cost construction leverages the texture loss map generated by a cost volume tensor to derive a more resilient texture loss.
The method, referred to as the occlusion-aware cost constructor (OCC), can be integrated with any cost construction method and significantly improves its accuracy.
Our experiments on four public light field datasets demonstrate that OCC, even when combined with a basic convolutional neural network depth estimator, outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on all metrics.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system to a single bilinear equation, then employing discrete geometry to derive various soliton solutions, and finally presenting a general solution in a specific configuration. Additionally, the analysis involves constructing Wronskian type solutions, solution transformations, and establishing the corresponding scattering problem within the context of the Ablowitz-Kaup-Ladik hierarchy.

By employing the Kaluza-Klein decomposition on a double field theory theory, we can derive a 4D non-Riemannian gravity model. The theory of double field theory, an extension of string theory, incorporates additional dimensions in its O(D,D) framework under the assumption of a flat O(D,D) structure. The gravitational model we developed emerges from a specific ansatz where the torus is replaced by a four-dimensional manifold with a non-degenerate O(4,4) structure. The resulting action yields a kinetic term and a mass-like term tied to a second rank tensor field. The kinetic term corresponds to a generalized non-Riemannian structure based on a single 4D form, akin to a generalized Dirac-Coulomb operator derived from a two-form field in a 6D space with non-degenerate O(2,2) structure. The mass-like term is analogous to a St\"uckelberg mechanism found in Hodge-Riemann structures. A secondary solution involving a single 4D form in a 8D manifold with O(4,4) structure is also explored, but it is found that such models lack kinetic terms.

In dense home WiFi networks, multiple access points and extenders often coexist within close proximity, creating significant interference issues.  IEEE 802.11v/co and 802.11k/v have been developed to help wireless devices avoid congestion, but initial drafts of these standards only focused on device density. Our research takes a different approach, focusing on the channel load an access point is experiencing, which is a more accurate indicator of interference. We use information from periodic broadcast scans and directed location updates to calculate the channel load each access point is carrying. Our findings indicate that selecting the access point with the lowest channel load is more effective than selecting the access point with the fewest connected devices, resulting in lower client dropouts and reduced client reconnection times. Our solution is highly compatible with current wireless standards, as it relies on standard management frames like beacon frames and directed location updates, enabling access points to inform clients about the actual channel load they're experiencing.
